prompts.text:
Would you please provide me the proof of

by Blekherman-Raymond, using the entropy method in LaTeX?

messages.text:
Would you please provide me the proof of 
t(P_5)^3 >= t(P_3)^5
by Blekherman-Raymond, using the entropy method in LaTeX?
I’ll locate the exact Blekherman–Raymond entropy argument first, then I’ll write it as a self-contained LaTeX proof with the same path convention they use.

Yes. With \(P_k\) denoting the path with **\(k\) edges**, the inequality
\[
t(P_5,W)^3\ge t(P_3,W)^5
\]
is the \(k=5,t=3\) case of the Erdős–Simonovits walk inequality. Blekherman–Raymond give a short alternative proof and rewrite it explicitly in entropy language in Section 4 of their paper. citeturn803318view0 Their convention is also that \(P_k\) has \(k\) edges. citeturn803318view0

The core construction is particularly clean in this \(P_3,P_5\) case: take a uniformly random \(P_3\)-homomorphism, and use its one-vertex and one-edge marginals to build three carefully folded \(P_5\)'s. The resulting entropy is exactly five times the entropy of the original \(P_3\)-homomorphism.

Here is a self-contained LaTeX version.

```latex
\begin{proposition}[Blekherman--Raymond, $P_3$--$P_5$ case]
Let $P_k$ denote the path with $k$ edges. Then, for every graphon $W$,
\[
    t(P_5,W)^3 \ge t(P_3,W)^5.
\]
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
We first prove the inequality for a finite graph $G$ on $n$ vertices.
Write
\[
    \hom(P_k,G):=|\Hom(P_k,G)|.
\]
The desired inequality
\[
    t(P_5,G)^3\ge t(P_3,G)^5
\]
is equivalent to
\[
    n^2 \hom(P_5,G)^3\ge \hom(P_3,G)^5,
\]
since $P_5$ has $6$ vertices and $P_3$ has $4$ vertices.

If $G$ has no edges, then both sides vanish, so there is nothing to prove.
Assume henceforth that $G$ has at least one edge.

Let
\[
    X=(X_0,X_1,X_2,X_3)
\]
be a uniformly random homomorphism from $P_3$ to $G$.
Thus $X$ is a uniformly random walk of length $3$ in $G$, and therefore
\[
    H(X_0,X_1,X_2,X_3)
    =
    \log |\Hom(P_3,G)|.
\]
The base of the logarithm is irrelevant.

We shall construct a random homomorphism from
\[
    F:=P_0\sqcup P_0\sqcup P_5\sqcup P_5\sqcup P_5
\]
to $G$ whose entropy is exactly $5H(X)$.
Since
\[
    |\Hom(F,G)|
    =
    n^2\hom(P_5,G)^3,
\]
the entropy bound
\[
    H(Y)\le \log|\Hom(F,G)|
\]
will then give the result.

\medskip

\noindent
\textbf{Step 1: the Markov property of the uniform random walk.}

The law of $X$ is uniform on all quadruples
$(x_0,x_1,x_2,x_3)$ satisfying
\[
    x_0x_1,\ x_1x_2,\ x_2x_3\in E(G).
\]
Consequently, conditioned on $X_i$, the variables on the two sides of
$X_i$ are conditionally independent.  In particular,
\[
    X_0 \perp (X_2,X_3)\mid X_1,
    \qquad
    (X_0,X_1)\perp X_3\mid X_2.
\]
Hence the entropy of $X$ satisfies the tree entropy identity
\begin{equation}\label{eq:tree-entropy-P3}
\begin{aligned}
    H(X)
    &=
    H(X_0,X_1)
    +H(X_1,X_2)
    +H(X_2,X_3)  \\
    &\qquad
    -H(X_1)-H(X_2).
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}

Indeed, by the chain rule and the conditional independences,
\[
\begin{aligned}
H(X_0,X_1,X_2,X_3)
&=
H(X_1)
+H(X_0\mid X_1)
+H(X_2\mid X_1)
+H(X_3\mid X_2) \\
&=
H(X_0,X_1)+H(X_1,X_2)+H(X_2,X_3)
-H(X_1)-H(X_2).
\end{aligned}
\]

\medskip

\noindent
\textbf{Step 2: three folds of $P_5$ onto $P_3$.}

Label the vertices of $P_3$ by
\[
    0,1,2,3
\]
in their natural order.

Consider the following three graph homomorphisms
$\phi_i:P_5\to P_3$, specified by the images of the six consecutive
vertices of $P_5$:
\[
\begin{aligned}
    \phi_1 &: (0,1,0,1,2,3),\\
    \phi_2 &: (0,1,2,1,2,3),\\
    \phi_3 &: (0,1,2,3,2,3).
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus $\phi_i$ traverses every edge of $P_3$ once, except for the
$i$th edge, which it traverses three times.

We now explain how to ``pull back'' the distribution of $X$ along
each $\phi_i$.

More generally, suppose
\[
    a_0,a_1,\dots,a_5\in\{0,1,2,3\}
\]
form a walk in $P_3$.  Define a random walk
\[
    Y=(Y_0,\dots,Y_5)
\]
in $G$ as follows.  First sample $Y_0$ with the same distribution as
$X_{a_0}$.  Having sampled $Y_j$, sample $Y_{j+1}$ according to the
conditional distribution
\[
    \mathbb P(Y_{j+1}=v\mid Y_j=u)
    :=
    \mathbb P(X_{a_{j+1}}=v\mid X_{a_j}=u).
\]
Then
\[
    Y_j\stackrel{d}{=}X_{a_j}
\]
for every $j$, and
\[
    (Y_j,Y_{j+1})
    \stackrel{d}{=}
    (X_{a_j},X_{a_{j+1}})
\]
for every $j$.
Moreover, $Y$ is supported on $\Hom(P_5,G)$.

Applying this construction to the three walks $\phi_1,\phi_2,\phi_3$
gives random homomorphisms
\[
    Y^{(1)},Y^{(2)},Y^{(3)}\in\Hom(P_5,G).
\]
We take these three random homomorphisms independently.

Finally, let $Z_0$ and $Z_3$ be independent random vertices having,
respectively, the distributions of $X_0$ and $X_3$, and independent
of all the $Y^{(i)}$.

Altogether,
\[
    Y:=(Z_0,Z_3,Y^{(1)},Y^{(2)},Y^{(3)})
\]
is a random element of $\Hom(F,G)$.

\medskip

\noindent
\textbf{Step 3: compute the entropy.}

For any Markov distribution on a path
$v_0v_1\cdots v_m$, one has
\begin{equation}\label{eq:tree-entropy}
    H(V_0,\dots,V_m)
    =
    \sum_{j=0}^{m-1}H(V_j,V_{j+1})
    -
    \sum_{j=1}^{m-1}H(V_j).
\end{equation}
This follows immediately from the chain rule:
\[
\begin{aligned}
H(V_0,\dots,V_m)
&=
H(V_0)+\sum_{j=0}^{m-1}H(V_{j+1}\mid V_j)\\
&=
H(V_0)+\sum_{j=0}^{m-1}
    \bigl(H(V_j,V_{j+1})-H(V_j)\bigr).
\end{aligned}
\]

We apply \eqref{eq:tree-entropy} to the three copies of $P_5$.

Across the three maps $\phi_1,\phi_2,\phi_3$, each edge
\[
    01,\qquad 12,\qquad 23
\]
of $P_3$ occurs exactly five times:
each occurs once in each $\phi_i$, and twice more in the unique
$\phi_i$ which backtracks over that edge.

Hence the positive edge contribution to
\[
    H(Y^{(1)})+H(Y^{(2)})+H(Y^{(3)})
\]
is
\[
    5H(X_0,X_1)
    +5H(X_1,X_2)
    +5H(X_2,X_3).
\]

It remains to count the internal vertices of the three copies of
$P_5$.  Their images under the three $\phi_i$ are
\[
\begin{array}{c|c}
\phi_1 & 1,0,1,2\\
\phi_2 & 1,2,1,2\\
\phi_3 & 1,2,3,2.
\end{array}
\]
Thus, among all internal vertices,
\[
    0\text{ occurs once},\qquad
    1\text{ occurs five times},\qquad
    2\text{ occurs five times},\qquad
    3\text{ occurs once}.
\]
Therefore
\begin{align*}
\sum_{i=1}^3 H(Y^{(i)})
&=
5H(X_0,X_1)+5H(X_1,X_2)+5H(X_2,X_3)\\
&\qquad
-H(X_0)-5H(X_1)-5H(X_2)-H(X_3).
\end{align*}

The two isolated vertices contribute
\[
    H(Z_0)+H(Z_3)=H(X_0)+H(X_3).
\]
Since all five components were chosen independently,
\[
\begin{aligned}
H(Y)
&=
H(Z_0)+H(Z_3)+\sum_{i=1}^3H(Y^{(i)})\\
&=
5\Bigl(
H(X_0,X_1)+H(X_1,X_2)+H(X_2,X_3)
-H(X_1)-H(X_2)
\Bigr).
\end{aligned}
\]
By \eqref{eq:tree-entropy-P3},
\[
    H(Y)=5H(X).
\]
Since $X$ is uniform on $\Hom(P_3,G)$,
\[
    H(Y)
    =
    5\log\hom(P_3,G).
\]

On the other hand, $Y$ is supported on $\Hom(F,G)$, so the
maximum-entropy bound gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
    5\log\hom(P_3,G)
    &=H(Y)\\
    &\le \log|\Hom(F,G)|\\
    &=\log\bigl(n^2\hom(P_5,G)^3\bigr).
\end{aligned}
\]
Exponentiating,
\[
    \hom(P_3,G)^5
    \le
    n^2\hom(P_5,G)^3.
\]
Dividing by $n^{20}$ yields
\[
    t(P_3,G)^5
    \le
    t(P_5,G)^3.
\]

Finally, the inequality extends from finite graphs to graphons by the
standard approximation of graphons by finite graphs together with
continuity of homomorphism densities.  Hence, for every graphon $W$,
\[
    \boxed{t(P_5,W)^3\ge t(P_3,W)^5}.
\]
\end{proof}
```

The important feature of the Blekherman–Raymond construction is the choice
\[
(0,1,0,1,2,3),\qquad
(0,1,2,1,2,3),\qquad
(0,1,2,3,2,3).
\]
Each edge of \(P_3\) then appears **exactly five times**, while after adding the two isolated endpoint vertices, each internal vertex entropy is subtracted exactly five times. This turns the entire entropy calculation into precisely
\[
5\bigl(H_{01}+H_{12}+H_{23}-H_1-H_2\bigr)=5H(X).
\]
That is the structural reason the exponents \(3\) and \(5\) appear.

Blekherman–Raymond state the general result \(t(P_k;G)^t\ge t(P_t;G)^k\) for odd \(k\ge t\), and Section 4 gives the entropy formulation used above. citeturn803318view0 The inequality itself is the Erdős–Simonovits conjecture, first proved by Sağlam; Blekherman–Raymond's contribution here is this substantially shorter alternative proof. citeturn803318view0

messages.text:
This article proves some lower bound on the graphon, using the entropy method.
I know that this does not naively relax to the arbitrary chordal graph. But I want to at least somehow extend it. Current condition is a bit restrictive. 
Do you have any idea to extend and relax the condition a bit?
I’ll isolate where purity enters the entropy argument, then test relaxations via variable clique sizes, local separator conditions, and maximal-clique decomposition.

The key obstruction is separator compatibility: unequal clique sizes make the local uniform clique laws inconsistent across adjacent bags. I’ll seek weaker hypotheses restoring this compatibility or controlling its entropy loss.
Two routes remain: preserve the same \(\Phi_H\) via a structural closure condition, or allow arbitrary chordal graphs with an entropy bound explicitly corrected for separator-marginal defects.

## Where purity is actually used

The chromatic-polynomial factorization is not the obstruction. Nor is the Moon–Moser step: it already controls every ratio \(t(K_r,W)/t(K_s,W)\). The restrictive point is the entropy construction. In the pure case, every bag uses the uniform law on \(\operatorname{Hom}(K_r,G)\), so the laws induced on a shared \(K_s\) agree automatically. This is exactly what makes the clique-tree gluing argument work. fileciteturn0file0L174-L206 fileciteturn0file0L209-L284

For unequal clique sizes, the uniform \(K_a\)- and \(K_b\)-laws generally induce different measures on their common separator. The triangle-with-many-leaves counterexample exploits precisely that mismatch. fileciteturn1file9L898-L904

There is, however, a way to restore compatibility without assuming that all maximal cliques have the same size:

> Instead of putting the uniform \(K_{r_i}\)-law on a maximal clique of size \(r_i\), put on it the \(r_i\)-coordinate marginal of one common uniform \(K_r\)-law, where \(r=\omega(H)\).

This loses some entropy, but the loss can be controlled by the same Moon–Moser ratios. The resulting theorem strictly extends the pure case.

---

# 1. The multiplicity profile of a chordal graph

Let \(H\) be a connected chordal graph with maximal cliques

\[
C_1,\ldots,C_m,
\qquad r_i:=|C_i|,
\]

and let \(T\) be a clique tree. For \(e=ij\in E(T)\), set

\[
S_e=C_i\cap C_j,\qquad s_e:=|S_e|.
\]

Put \(r=\omega(H)=\max_i r_i\), and for \(1\le j\le r\) define

\[
b_j
:=
\#\{i:r_i\ge j\}
-
\#\{e:s_e\ge j\}.
\tag{1}
\]

Using the usual chordal factorization,

\[
\chi_H(x)
=
\frac{\prod_i (x)_{r_i}}
     {\prod_e (x)_{s_e}},
\]

we obtain

\[
\chi_H(x)
=
\prod_{j=1}^{r}(x-j+1)^{b_j}.
\tag{2}
\]

Thus \(b_j\) is the multiplicity of \(x-j+1\) as a factor of \(\chi_H(x)\), so it is independent of the chosen clique tree.

Write

\[
q:=1-p,
\qquad
c_j(p):=1-(j-1)q.
\]

Then

\[
\Phi_H(p)
=
q^{v(H)}\chi_H(1/q)
=
\prod_{j=1}^{r}c_j(p)^{b_j}.
\tag{3}
\]

For a pure \(r\)-chordal graph,

\[
b_{j+1}-b_j
=
\#\{e:s_e=j\}\ge 0,
\]

so the sequence \(b_1,\ldots,b_r\) is automatically nondecreasing. Purity is therefore sufficient for a more intrinsic property of the chromatic factorization.

---

# 2. A genuine extension of the theorem

## Theorem

Let \(H\) be a connected chordal graph with clique number \(r\ge 3\). Define \(b_1,\ldots,b_r\) by (1), equivalently by (2). Suppose that

\[
b_1\le b_2\le\cdots\le b_r.
\tag{4}
\]

Then every graphon \(W\) with

\[
p=t(K_2,W)\ge 1-\frac1{r-1}
\]

satisfies

\[
t(H,W)\ge \Phi_H(p)
=
(1-p)^{v(H)}
\chi_H\!\left(\frac1{1-p}\right).
\tag{5}
\]

This contains every connected pure chordal graph, but it also contains genuinely non-pure chordal graphs.

---

# 3. Proof

It is enough first to prove the result for finite graphs and then pass to graphons by sampling or step-graphon approximation.

Let \(G\) be a finite graph on \(n\) vertices, and write

\[
h_j:=\operatorname{hom}(K_j,G),
\qquad
t_j:=\frac{h_j}{n^j}.
\]

Assume first that

\[
p>1-\frac1{r-1}.
\]

Then Moon–Moser gives \(t_r>0\). Let

\[
Y=(Y_1,\ldots,Y_r)
\]

be uniformly distributed on \(\operatorname{Hom}(K_r,G)\). For \(0\le j\le r\), put

\[
\mathcal H_j:=H(Y_1,\ldots,Y_j),
\qquad
\mathcal H_0:=0,
\]

and define the successive conditional entropies

\[
\alpha_j:=\mathcal H_j-\mathcal H_{j-1}
=
H(Y_j\mid Y_1,\ldots,Y_{j-1}).
\tag{6}
\]

Because \(Y\) is exchangeable, the entropy of any \(j\)-coordinate marginal equals \(\mathcal H_j\).

For every maximal clique \(C_i\), put on \(\operatorname{Hom}(C_i,G)\) the law of an arbitrary \(r_i\)-coordinate marginal of \(Y\). These local laws have matching separator marginals, because all of them come from the same exchangeable \(K_r\)-law. The junction-tree entropy construction therefore gives

\[
\log\operatorname{hom}(H,G)
\ge
\sum_i\mathcal H_{r_i}
-
\sum_{e\in E(T)}\mathcal H_{s_e}.
\tag{7}
\]

Expanding each \(\mathcal H_k=\sum_{j\le k}\alpha_j\) and using (1),

\[
\sum_i\mathcal H_{r_i}
-
\sum_e\mathcal H_{s_e}
=
\sum_{j=1}^{r}b_j\alpha_j.
\tag{8}
\]

Also,

\[
v(H)
=
\sum_i r_i-\sum_e s_e
=
\sum_{j=1}^{r}b_j.
\tag{9}
\]

Define the entropy deficits

\[
\delta_j:=\log n-\alpha_j.
\tag{10}
\]

Since a single vertex takes at most \(n\) values,

\[
\delta_j\ge 0.
\]

Normalizing (7) by \(n^{v(H)}\), equations (8)–(10) give

\[
\log t(H,G)
\ge
-\sum_{j=1}^{r}b_j\delta_j.
\tag{11}
\]

We now control the suffix sums of the \(\delta_j\). For \(0\le k<r\),

\[
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{j=k+1}^{r}\delta_j
&=
(r-k)\log n-(\mathcal H_r-\mathcal H_k)\\
&=
(r-k)\log n-\log h_r+\mathcal H_k\\
&\le
(r-k)\log n-\log h_r+\log h_k\\
&=
-\log\frac{t_r}{t_k}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{12}
\]

Here \(t_0=t_1=1\). By the Moon–Moser clique-ratio inequalities,

\[
\frac{t_r}{t_k}
\ge
\frac{A_r(p)}{A_k(p)}
=
\prod_{j=k+1}^{r}c_j(p).
\tag{13}
\]

Consequently,

\[
\sum_{j=k+1}^{r}\delta_j
\le
\sum_{j=k+1}^{r}\lambda_j,
\qquad
\lambda_j:=-\log c_j(p).
\tag{14}
\]

Because \(b_1\le\cdots\le b_r\), summation by parts gives

\[
\sum_{j=1}^{r}b_j\delta_j
=
b_1\sum_{j=1}^{r}\delta_j
+
\sum_{k=1}^{r-1}
(b_{k+1}-b_k)
\sum_{j=k+1}^{r}\delta_j.
\tag{15}
\]

All coefficients on the right are nonnegative. Applying (14),

\[
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{j=1}^{r}b_j\delta_j
&\le
b_1\sum_{j=1}^{r}\lambda_j
+
\sum_{k=1}^{r-1}
(b_{k+1}-b_k)
\sum_{j=k+1}^{r}\lambda_j\\
&=
\sum_{j=1}^{r}b_j\lambda_j\\
&=
-\log\prod_{j=1}^{r}c_j(p)^{b_j}\\
&=
-\log\Phi_H(p).
\end{aligned}
\tag{16}
\]

Combining (11) and (16),

\[
\log t(H,G)\ge \log\Phi_H(p),
\]

which proves

\[
t(H,G)\ge\Phi_H(p).
\]

At the boundary \(p=1-1/(r-1)\), one has \(c_r(p)=0\). Since \(b_r\ge1\), the right-hand side is zero, so the statement is immediate. The passage from finite graphs to graphons is standard.

---

# 4. A simple structural interpretation

Let

\[
m_j:=\#\{\text{maximal cliques of size exactly }j\},
\]

and let

\[
a_j:=\#\{\text{clique-tree edges }e:s_e=j\}.
\]

Then directly from (1),

\[
b_{j+1}-b_j
=
a_j-m_j.
\tag{17}
\]

Therefore condition (4) is equivalent to

\[
m_j\le a_j
\qquad
(1\le j<r).
\tag{18}
\]

For a connected nontrivial chordal graph, \(m_1=0\), so the substantive conditions begin at \(j=2\).

Thus smaller maximal cliques are allowed, provided that, at every size \(j\), they are compensated by at least as many separators of size \(j\). Purity is the special case \(m_j=0\) for every \(j<r\).

### Example: triangles plus a maximal edge

Take two triangles sharing an edge, and attach one pendant edge to one of the remaining triangle vertices. Its maximal cliques have sizes

\[
3,3,2,
\]

and a clique tree has separator sizes

\[
2,1.
\]

Hence

\[
(b_1,b_2,b_3)=(1,2,2),
\]

which is nondecreasing. The graph is not pure, but the theorem gives, for every \(p\ge1/2\),

\[
t(H,W)
\ge
p^2(2p-1)^2.
\tag{19}
\]

Indeed,

\[
\chi_H(x)=x(x-1)^2(x-2)^2.
\]

More generally, for a chordal graph with clique number \(3\), let \(m_2\) be the number of maximal edges and let \(a_2\) be the number of edges of the clique tree corresponding to two triangles intersecting in an edge. Then

\[
t(H,W)\ge\Phi_H(p),\qquad p\ge\frac12,
\]

whenever

\[
m_2\le a_2.
\tag{20}
\]

This allows a linear number of maximal edges, rather than requiring none.

---

# 5. An explicit lower bound for every chordal graph

The same construction still gives something when \(b_1,\ldots,b_r\) is not nondecreasing.

The conditional entropies \(\alpha_j\) in (6) are nonincreasing. Indeed,

\[
\begin{aligned}
\alpha_{j+1}
&=
H(Y_{j+1}\mid Y_1,\ldots,Y_j)\\
&\le
H(Y_{j+1}\mid Y_2,\ldots,Y_j)\\
&=
H(Y_j\mid Y_1,\ldots,Y_{j-1})
=
\alpha_j,
\end{aligned}
\]

where the equality uses exchangeability. Hence

\[
0\le\delta_1\le\delta_2\le\cdots\le\delta_r.
\tag{21}
\]

Now modify \(b=(b_1,\ldots,b_r)\) as follows. Whenever two consecutive constant blocks have decreasing averages, merge them and replace all entries in the merged block by their common average. Continue until the resulting sequence

\[
\bar b_1\le\bar b_2\le\cdots\le\bar b_r
\tag{22}
\]

is nondecreasing. This is the standard adjacent-block averaging procedure.

For every nondecreasing sequence \(\delta\),

\[
\sum_j b_j\delta_j
\le
\sum_j\bar b_j\delta_j.
\tag{23}
\]

Applying the suffix bounds (14) to the nondecreasing sequence \(\bar b\) gives

\[
\sum_j\bar b_j\delta_j
\le
\sum_j\bar b_j\lambda_j.
\]

Therefore every connected chordal graph satisfies the explicit bound

\[
\boxed{
t(H,W)
\ge
\prod_{j=1}^{r}
\left(1-(j-1)(1-p)\right)^{\bar b_j}
}
\tag{24}
\]

for

\[
p\ge1-\frac1{r-1}.
\]

When \(b\) is already nondecreasing, \(\bar b=b\), and (24) is exactly the chromatic-polynomial bound. When it is not, (24) supplies a precise entropy penalty for the failure of purity.

For example, if \(H_L\) is a triangle with \(L\) leaves attached to each triangle vertex, then

\[
b=(1,3L+1,1).
\]

The block averaging gives

\[
\bar b=
\left(
1,\frac{3L+2}{2},\frac{3L+2}{2}
\right),
\]

and hence

\[
t(H_L,W)
\ge
\bigl[p(2p-1)\bigr]^{(3L+2)/2},
\qquad p\ge\frac12.
\tag{25}
\]

This does not recover

\[
\Phi_{H_L}(p)=p^{3L+1}(2p-1),
\]

which is consistent with the known counterexample, but it remains an explicit one-variable lower bound valid for all such graphons.

---

## Assessment

The most natural relaxation is therefore not “arbitrary chordal,” but:

\[
\boxed{
\text{the multiplicities of }
x,x-1,\ldots,x-r+1
\text{ in }\chi_H(x)
\text{ are nondecreasing}.
}
\]

This condition:

- strictly contains the pure chordal class;
- has the transparent clique-tree formulation \(m_j\le a_j\);
- retains the original threshold \(p\ge1-1/(r-1)\);
- gives exactly the same chromatic-polynomial lower bound;
- and comes directly from a modified entropy construction, rather than from a separate argument.

For graphs outside this class, the averaged profile \(\bar b\) gives a canonical corrected lower bound. To recover \(\Phi_H\) beyond the nondecreasing regime, one would need information not contained in the Moon–Moser clique ratios alone—most likely a nonuniform common \(K_r\)-law or a rooted clique-extension inequality controlling how much the smaller-bag marginal can differ from the \(K_r\)-marginal.
Interesting. Would you please write this proof as a LaTeX, complete, flawless, detailed?

I’ll also verify the graphon limit passage explicitly and format the final result as a compilable `.tex` source.
The core theorem survives the audit: suffix-sum bounds for the entropy deficits combine with monotone chromatic-factor multiplicities through summation by parts with nonnegative coefficients.

**# Prompt for ChatGPT Pro: resolve one open case of the chromatic-polynomial lower bound**

You are a research mathematician specializing in extremal graph theory and graph limits. Below is a fully precise open problem with 21 concrete instances. Your task: **\*\*completely resolve at least one instance\*\*** — either by a rigorous proof or by an explicit, exactly verifiable counterexample. You choose which instance and which direction; both outcomes are equally valuable. Partial progress is welcome as a secondary output, but the goal is one full resolution.

**## 1. Definitions (all standard, stated to fix conventions)**

A **\*\*graphon\*\*** is a symmetric Lebesgue-measurable function $W:[0,1]^2\to[0,1]$. For a finite simple graph $H$ with vertex set $V(H)$ and edge set $E(H)$, the **\*\*homomorphism density\*\*** is

$$

 t(H,W) \\;=\\; \int\_{[0,1]^{V(H)}} \prod\_{uv\in E(H)} W(x\_u,x\_v)\\; \prod\_{u\in V(H)} dx\_u .

$$

(Maps are not required to be injective.) The **\*\*edge density\*\*** of $W$ is $p := t(K\_2,W) = \iint W$.

For a graph $H$ with chromatic polynomial $\chi\_H$ and $v = v(H)$ vertices, define for $0\le p<1$

$$

 \Phi\_H(p) \\;:=\\; (1-p)^{v}\\,\chi\_H\\!\left(\frac{1}{1-p}\right),

 \qquad \Phi\_H(1):=1 \ \text{(continuous extension)}.

$$

This is a polynomial in $p$ with integer coefficients (expanded forms are given below for each instance).

**\*\*Conjectured inequality for a given $H$\*\*** (this is the object to prove or disprove):

\> For every graphon $W$ with edge density $p = t(K\_2,W) \ge 1 - \dfrac{1}{\chi(H)-1}$, it holds that $t(H,W)\ \ge\ \Phi\_H(p)$.

Here $\chi(H)$ is the chromatic number. The density restriction is essential: below the threshold the inequality is generally false and is not conjectured.

Equivalent finite form: since finite graphs are dense in the graphon space and both sides are continuous in the relevant densities, the statement for $H$ is equivalent to: for every finite simple graph $G$ (with $t(F,G) := \hom(F,G)/n^{v(F)}$, so $t(K\_2,G)=2e(G)/n^2$), $t(K\_2,G)\ge$ threshold implies $t(H,G)\ge\Phi\_H(t(K\_2,G))$. You may work in either setting. For a **\*\*counterexample\*\*** you may restrict to step graphons without loss of generality: if $W$ is a step function with $k$ parts of measures $\alpha\_1,\dots,\alpha\_k$ ($\sum\alpha\_i=1$) and symmetric value matrix $M\in[0,1]^{k\times k}$, then

$$

 t(H,W) = \sum\_{\varphi\:V(H)\to[k]}\ \prod\_{uv\in E(H)} M\_{\varphi(u)\varphi(v)}\ \prod\_{u\in V(H)}\alpha\_{\varphi(u)} .

$$

**## 2. Hard constraints any answer must respect**

**\*\*(a) Infinitely many equality cases.\*\*** Let $T\_k$ denote the balanced Turán graphon ($k$ equal parts, $W=0$ on the $k$ diagonal blocks, $W=1$ off-diagonal), with $p = 1-1/k$. Then $t(H,T\_k)=\chi\_H(k)/k^{v(H)}$ and $\Phi\_H(1-1/k)=\chi\_H(k)/k^{v(H)}$ — **\*\*equality holds at $T\_k$ for every $k \ge \chi(H)-1$\*\***, and also at $W\equiv 1$. A proof cannot afford any loss at these points; a counterexample must do strictly better than all of them.

**\*\*(b) The inequality is false for some $H$.\*\*** Among all 117 non-bipartite graphs on $\le 6$ vertices (no isolated vertices, no isolated-edge components), 23 have exact counterexamples and 73 have accepted proofs; the 21 below are exactly the unresolved ones. Known counterexamples come in two shapes: (i) tensor products $W = T\_{k\_1}\otimes\cdots\otimes T\_{k\_s}$ (for which $p=\prod\_i(1-1/k\_i)$ and $t(H,W)=\prod\_i \chi\_H(k\_i)/k\_i^{v(H)}$), and (ii) local perturbations of $T\_2$ or $T\_3$, including one genuinely 5-step "fractional-fibre" perturbation of $T\_2$ at $p\approx 1/2$. So no general theorem is possible; the structure of the specific $H$ must be used.

**\*\*(c) What has already been ruled out for all 21 instances below.\*\*** Do not spend effort re-deriving these:

\- **\*\*Tensor counterexamples are exhausted\*\***: all $T\_{k\_1}\otimes T\_{k\_2}$ with $k\_i\le 500$, repeated and consecutive products with endpoints $\le 1000$, and $2\times10^6$ random products of lengths 2–24 with factors $\le 5000$ were checked in exact arithmetic. None violates the inequality for these 21 graphs.

\- **\*\*Local stability holds\*\***: for each of the 21 graphs there is a proven explicit $L^\infty$-radius around every interior Turán graphon $T\_k$, $k\ge\chi(H)$, and around the critical threshold Turán graphon, inside which the inequality holds. So a counterexample cannot be an $L^\infty$-small perturbation of any balanced Turán graphon. (Perturbations of small measure but order-one amplitude are *\*not\** excluded in general — that is how the one known non-tensor 6-vertex counterexample works.)

\- **\*\*The high-density endpoint is closed\*\***: for each of the 21 graphs there is a proven explicit $\varepsilon\_H>0$ such that the inequality holds for **\*\*every\*\*** graphon with $1-p\le\varepsilon\_H$. (The proven radii are small, e.g. of order $10^{-6}$ to $10^{-12}$.) So a counterexample must live at "middle" densities; a proof, however, should ideally cover the whole range on its own.

\- **\*\*The constant graphon is safe\*\***: $W\equiv p$ satisfies the inequality strictly in the open range for all 21 graphs.

**\*\*(d) Rigor standard.\*\*** A proof must be complete and self-contained modulo the citable literature (e.g. Goodman's bound, Moon–Moser clique-density inequalities $t\_{j}\ge t\_{j-1}\bigl(1-(j-1)(1-p)\bigr)$, Kruskal–Katona, Reiher's clique density theorem, standard entropy/Cauchy–Schwarz/Hölder arguments, Lovász's graph-limits book). Numerical SDP/flag-algebra output is acceptable **\*\*only\*\*** if rounded to an exact rational certificate that can be verified by hand or exact arithmetic. A counterexample must be an explicit step graphon with rational part sizes and rational values, an explicit rational $p$ in the admissible range, and an exact rational evaluation of both $t(H,W)$ and $\Phi\_H(p)$ exhibiting $t(H,W)<\Phi\_H(p)$.

**## 3. The 21 open instances**

Vertices are labeled $0,\dots,v-1$. "Threshold" is $1-1/(\chi(H)-1)$; the inequality is claimed exactly on $p\in[\text{threshold},1]$. The graph6 string is authoritative machine-readable identification; the edge list is the same graph spelled out. ($\bar H$ = complement, listed since several methods work in the complement at high density.)

**### Five-vertex instance**

**\*\*Atlas 43\*\*** — graph6 \`Dlc\`, $v=5$, $e=6$, $\chi=3$, threshold $p\ge 1/2$. The "house": 5-cycle $0\\!-\\!1\\!-\\!2\\!-\\!3\\!-\\!4\\!-\\!0$ plus chord $\\{0,3\\}$.

Edges: $\\{0,1\\},\\{0,3\\},\\{0,4\\},\\{1,2\\},\\{2,3\\},\\{3,4\\}$.

$\chi\_H(x)=x(x-1)(x-2)(x^2-3x+3)$; target $\Phi\_H(p)=p(2p-1)(3p^2-3p+1)=6p^4-9p^3+5p^2-p$.

$\bar H$ edges: $\\{0,2\\},\\{1,3\\},\\{1,4\\},\\{2,4\\}$.

**### Six-vertex instances, $\chi=3$ (threshold $p\ge 1/2$)**

**\*\*Atlas 118\*\*** — graph6 \`Eht?\`, $e=7$.

Edges: $\\{0,1\\},\\{0,4\\},\\{1,2\\},\\{1,4\\},\\{1,5\\},\\{2,3\\},\\{3,4\\}$.

$\chi\_H(x)=x(x-1)^2(x-2)(x^2-3x+3)$; $\Phi\_H(p)=p^2(2p-1)(3p^2-3p+1)$.

$\bar H$: $\\{0,2\\},\\{0,3\\},\\{0,5\\},\\{1,3\\},\\{2,4\\},\\{2,5\\},\\{3,5\\},\\{4,5\\}$.

**\*\*Atlas 122\*\*** — graph6 \`Eld?\`, $e=7$.

Edges: $\\{0,1\\},\\{0,3\\},\\{0,4\\},\\{1,2\\},\\{1,5\\},\\{2,3\\},\\{3,4\\}$.

$\chi\_H(x)=x(x-1)^2(x-2)(x^2-3x+3)$; $\Phi\_H(p)=p^2(2p-1)(3p^2-3p+1)$.

$\bar H$: $\\{0,2\\},\\{0,5\\},\\{1,3\\},\\{1,4\\},\\{2,4\\},\\{2,5\\},\\{3,5\\},\\{4,5\\}$.

**\*\*Atlas 124\*\*** — graph6 \`Exd?\`, $e=7$.

Edges: $\\{0,1\\},\\{0,2\\},\\{0,4\\},\\{1,2\\},\\{1,5\\},\\{2,3\\},\\{3,4\\}$.

$\chi\_H(x)=x(x-1)^2(x-2)(x^2-3x+3)$; $\Phi\_H(p)=p^2(2p-1)(3p^2-3p+1)$.

$\bar H$: $\\{0,3\\},\\{0,5\\},\\{1,3\\},\\{1,4\\},\\{2,4\\},\\{2,5\\},\\{3,5\\},\\{4,5\\}$.

**\*\*Atlas 127\*\*** — graph6 \`EZEG\`, $e=7$. A 6-cycle $0\\!-\\!2\\!-\\!1\\!-\\!3\\!-\\!4\\!-\\!5\\!-\\!0$ plus chord $\\{2,3\\}$.

Edges: $\\{0,2\\},\\{0,5\\},\\{1,2\\},\\{1,3\\},\\{2,3\\},\\{3,4\\},\\{4,5\\}$.

$\chi\_H(x)=x(x-1)(x-2)^2(x^2-2x+2)$; $\Phi\_H(p)=p(2p-1)^2(2p^2-2p+1)$.

$\bar H$: $\\{0,1\\},\\{0,3\\},\\{0,4\\},\\{1,4\\},\\{1,5\\},\\{2,4\\},\\{2,5\\},\\{3,5\\}$.

**\*\*Atlas 130\*\*** — graph6 \`E{CW\`, $e=7$. **\*\*Chordal.\*\*** Two vertex-disjoint triangles $\\{0,1,2\\}$ and $\\{3,4,5\\}$ joined by the single bridge $\\{0,3\\}$.

Edges: $\\{0,1\\},\\{0,2\\},\\{0,3\\},\\{1,2\\},\\{3,4\\},\\{3,5\\},\\{4,5\\}$.

$\chi\_H(x)=x(x-1)^3(x-2)^2$; $\Phi\_H(p)=p^3(2p-1)^2$.

Useful bilinear form: $t(H,W)=\iint W(x,y)\\,\tau(x)\\,\tau(y)\\,dx\\,dy$ where $\tau(x):=\iint W(x,a)W(x,b)W(a,b)\\,da\\,db$ is the rooted-triangle density.

$\bar H$: $\\{0,4\\},\\{0,5\\},\\{1,3\\},\\{1,4\\},\\{1,5\\},\\{2,3\\},\\{2,4\\},\\{2,5\\}$.

**\*\*Atlas 147\*\*** — graph6 \`EhMg\`, $e=8$.

Edges: $\\{0,1\\},\\{0,5\\},\\{1,2\\},\\{2,3\\},\\{2,4\\},\\{2,5\\},\\{3,4\\},\\{4,5\\}$.

$\chi\_H(x)=x(x-1)(x-2)^2(x^2-3x+3)$; $\Phi\_H(p)=p(2p-1)^2(3p^2-3p+1)$.

Edges: $\\{0,1\\},\\{0,4\\},\\{1,2\\},\\{1,5\\},\\{2,3\\},\\{3,4\\},\\{3,5\\},\\{4,5\\}$.

$\chi\_H(x)=x(x-1)(x-2)^2(x^2-3x+4)$; $\Phi\_H(p)=p(2p-1)^2(4p^2-5p+2)$.

$\bar H$: $\\{0,2\\},\\{0,3\\},\\{0,5\\},\\{1,3\\},\\{1,4\\},\\{2,4\\},\\{2,5\\}$.

**\*\*Atlas 153\*\*** — graph6 \`Ehf\_\`, $e=8$. *\*Density-neutral: $\Phi\_H(p)\le 0$ for $1/2\le p\le 7/12$, so only $p>7/12$ is at issue.\**

Edges: $\\{0,1\\},\\{0,4\\},\\{0,5\\},\\{1,2\\},\\{1,5\\},\\{2,3\\},\\{2,5\\},\\{3,4\\}$.

Edges: $\\{0,2\\},\\{0,3\\},\\{0,5\\},\\{1,2\\},\\{1,3\\},\\{2,3\\},\\{2,4\\},\\{3,4\\},\\{4,5\\}$.

$\bar H$: $\\{0,2\\},\\{0,3\\},\\{1,3\\},\\{1,4\\},\\{1,5\\},\\{2,4\\}$.

**\*\*Atlas 174\*\*** — graph6 \`EtTg\`, $e=9$. The **\*\*triangular prism\*\*** $K\_3\\,\square\\,K\_2$: triangles $\\{0,2,3\\}$, $\\{1,4,5\\}$, matching $\\{0,1\\},\\{2,5\\},\\{3,4\\}$. 3-regular. *\*Density-neutral: only $p>7/12$ is at issue.\**

Edges: $\\{0,1\\},\\{0,2\\},\\{0,3\\},\\{1,4\\},\\{1,5\\},\\{2,3\\},\\{2,5\\},\\{3,4\\},\\{4,5\\}$.

$\chi\_H(x)=x(x-1)(x-2)(x^3-6x^2+14x-13)$; $\Phi\_H(p)=p(2p-1)(13p^3-25p^2+17p-4)$.

$\bar H$: $\\{0,4\\},\\{0,5\\},\\{1,2\\},\\{1,3\\},\\{2,4\\},\\{3,5\\}$ — the complement is the 6-cycle $4\\!-\\!0\\!-\\!5\\!-\\!3\\!-\\!1\\!-\\!2\\!-\\!4$ (the prism is $\bar{C\_6}$).

Integer values: $\chi\_H(3)=12$, $\chi\_H(4)=264$.

**\*\*Atlas 188\*\*** — graph6 \`EzNG\`, $e=10$. *\*Density-neutral: only $p>7/12$ is at issue.\**

Edges: $\\{0,1\\},\\{0,2\\},\\{0,5\\},\\{1,2\\},\\{1,3\\},\\{1,5\\},\\{2,3\\},\\{2,4\\},\\{3,4\\},\\{4,5\\}$.

$\chi\_H(x)=x(x-1)(x-2)(x^3-7x^2+18x-17)$; $\Phi\_H(p)=p(2p-1)(17p^3-33p^2+22p-5)$.

$\bar H$: $\\{0,3\\},\\{0,4\\},\\{1,4\\},\\{2,5\\},\\{3,5\\}$.

**### Six-vertex instances, $\chi=4$ (threshold $p\ge 2/3$)**

**\*\*Atlas 157\*\*** — graph6 \`\`E\~\`\_\`\`, $e=9$. **\*\*Chordal.\*\*** $K\_4$ on $\\{0,1,2,3\\}$, a triangle $\\{1,2,5\\}$ glued along edge $\\{1,2\\}$, and a pendant vertex $4$ attached to $0$.

Edges: $\\{0,1\\},\\{0,2\\},\\{0,3\\},\\{0,4\\},\\{1,2\\},\\{1,3\\},\\{1,5\\},\\{2,3\\},\\{2,5\\}$.

$\chi\_H(x)=x(x-1)^2(x-2)^2(x-3)$; $\Phi\_H(p)=p^2(2p-1)^2(3p-2)$.

$\bar H$: $\\{0,5\\},\\{1,4\\},\\{2,4\\},\\{3,4\\},\\{3,5\\},\\{4,5\\}$.

**\*\*Atlas 169\*\*** — graph6 \`Exf\_\`, $e=9$.

Edges: $\\{0,1\\},\\{0,2\\},\\{0,4\\},\\{0,5\\},\\{1,2\\},\\{1,5\\},\\{2,3\\},\\{2,5\\},\\{3,4\\}$.

$\chi\_H(x)=x(x-1)(x-2)(x-3)(x^2-3x+3)$; $\Phi\_H(p)=p(2p-1)(3p-2)(3p^2-3p+1)$.

$\bar H$: $\\{0,3\\},\\{1,3\\},\\{1,4\\},\\{2,4\\},\\{3,5\\},\\{4,5\\}$.

Edges: $\\{0,2\\},\\{0,3\\},\\{0,4\\},\\{0,5\\},\\{1,2\\},\\{1,3\\},\\{2,3\\},\\{2,4\\},\\{3,4\\},\\{4,5\\}$.

$\chi\_H(x)=x(x-1)(x-2)^3(x-3)$; $\Phi\_H(p)=p(2p-1)^3(3p-2)$.

$\bar H$: $\\{0,1\\},\\{1,4\\},\\{1,5\\},\\{2,5\\},\\{3,5\\}$.

**\*\*Atlas 185\*\*** — graph6 \`Exv\_\`, $e=10$.

Edges: $\\{0,1\\},\\{0,2\\},\\{0,4\\},\\{0,5\\},\\{1,2\\},\\{1,4\\},\\{1,5\\},\\{2,3\\},\\{2,5\\},\\{3,4\\}$.

$\chi\_H(x)=x(x-1)(x-2)(x-3)(x^2-4x+5)$; $\Phi\_H(p)=p(2p-1)(3p-2)(5p^2-6p+2)$.

$\bar H$: $\\{0,3\\},\\{1,3\\},\\{2,4\\},\\{3,5\\},\\{4,5\\}$.

**\*\*Atlas 194\*\*** — graph6 \`E\~wW\`, $e=11$. $K\_5$ minus an edge on $\\{0,1,2,3,4\\}$ (missing $\\{3,4\\}$), plus vertex $5$ adjacent to $3,4$.

Edges: $\\{0,1\\},\\{0,2\\},\\{0,3\\},\\{0,4\\},\\{1,2\\},\\{1,3\\},\\{1,4\\},\\{2,3\\},\\{2,4\\},\\{3,5\\},\\{4,5\\}$.

$\chi\_H(x)=x(x-1)(x-2)(x-3)(x^2-5x+7)$; $\Phi\_H(p)=p(2p-1)(3p-2)(7p^2-9p+3)$.

$\bar H$: $\\{0,5\\},\\{1,5\\},\\{2,5\\},\\{3,4\\}$.

**\*\*Atlas 196\*\*** — graph6 \`ER\~g\`, $e=11$.

Edges: $\\{0,2\\},\\{0,4\\},\\{0,5\\},\\{1,3\\},\\{1,4\\},\\{1,5\\},\\{2,3\\},\\{2,4\\},\\{2,5\\},\\{3,4\\},\\{4,5\\}$.

$\chi\_H(x)=x(x-1)(x-2)(x-3)(x^2-5x+7)$; $\Phi\_H(p)=p(2p-1)(3p-2)(7p^2-9p+3)$.

$\bar H$: $\\{0,1\\},\\{0,3\\},\\{1,2\\},\\{3,5\\}$.

**\*\*Atlas 199\*\*** — graph6 \`El^g\`, $e=11$.

Edges: $\\{0,1\\},\\{0,3\\},\\{0,5\\},\\{1,2\\},\\{1,4\\},\\{1,5\\},\\{2,3\\},\\{2,4\\},\\{2,5\\},\\{3,4\\},\\{4,5\\}$.

$\chi\_H(x)=x(x-1)(x-2)(x-3)(x^2-5x+8)$; $\Phi\_H(p)=p(2p-1)(3p-2)(8p^2-11p+4)$.

$\bar H$: $\\{0,2\\},\\{0,4\\},\\{1,3\\},\\{3,5\\}$.

**\*\*Atlas 203\*\*** — graph6 \`E\~^G\`, $e=12$.

Edges: $\\{0,1\\},\\{0,2\\},\\{0,3\\},\\{0,5\\},\\{1,2\\},\\{1,3\\},\\{1,4\\},\\{1,5\\},\\{2,3\\},\\{2,4\\},\\{3,4\\},\\{4,5\\}$.

$\chi\_H(x)=x(x-1)(x-2)(x-3)(x^2-6x+10)$; $\Phi\_H(p)=p(2p-1)(3p-2)(10p^2-14p+5)$.

$\bar H$: $\\{0,4\\},\\{2,5\\},\\{3,5\\}$.

**## 4. Known partial lower bounds on the three chordal instances**

For connected chordal $H$ with maximal clique sizes $r\_i$ and clique-tree separator sizes $s\_e$, write $b\_j := \\#\\{i: r\_i\ge j\\} - \\#\\{e: s\_e \ge j\\}$ (so $\chi\_H(x)=\prod\_j (x-j+1)^{b\_j}$), and $c\_j(p) := 1-(j-1)(1-p)$. An entropy argument (uniform $K\_r$-homomorphism law, junction-tree gluing, Moon–Moser suffix bounds) proves $t(H,W)\ge \prod\_j c\_j(p)^{b\_j}=\Phi\_H(p)$ whenever $b\_1\le\cdots\le b\_r$ — but all three chordal instances above **\*\*violate\*\*** that monotonicity, and the same method then only yields the strictly weaker "pooled" bound $\prod\_j c\_j(p)^{\bar b\_j}$ with $\bar b$ the isotonic (pool-adjacent-violators) regression of $b$:

\- **\*\*Atlas 130\*\***: $b=(1,3,2)$, proven bound $t \ge \bigl[p(2p-1)\bigr]^{5/2}$, target $p^3(2p-1)^2$.

\- **\*\*Atlas 157\*\***: $b=(1,2,2,1)$, $\bar b=(1,\tfrac53,\tfrac53,\tfrac53)$, proven bound $t \ge \bigl[p(2p-1)(3p-2)\bigr]^{5/3}$; target $p^2(2p-1)^2(3p-2)$.

\- **\*\*Atlas 181\*\***: $b=(1,1,3,1)$, $\bar b=(1,1,2,2)$, proven bound $t \ge p\\,(2p-1)^2(3p-2)^2$; target $p(2p-1)^3(3p-2)$. **\*\*The gap is a single factor $(3p-2)$ vs $(2p-1)$.\*\*** Closing this one factor resolves the instance.

**## 5. Suggested entry points (you are free to ignore these)**

1\. **\*\*Atlas 130\*\*** (two triangles joined by a bridge). The cleanest statement in the list: prove or disprove $\iint W(x,y)\tau(x)\tau(y) \ge p^3(2p-1)^2$ for $p\ge 1/2$, where $\tau$ is the rooted-triangle density and $\int\tau = t(K\_3,W) \ge p(2p-1)$ by Goodman's bound. The difficulty is the correlation between $W(x,y)$ and the product $\tau(x)\tau(y)$; naive Cauchy–Schwarz decouplings lose at $T\_k$.

2\. **\*\*Atlas 181\*\***: upgrade the pooled entropy bound by one factor (see §4).

3\. **\*\*Atlas 43\*\*** (the house): the only 5-vertex instance; $t \ge p(2p-1)(3p^2-3p+1)$ for $p\ge 1/2$. **# Prompt for ChatGPT Pro: resolve one open case of the chromatic-polynomial lower bound**

You are a research mathematician specializing in extremal graph theory and graph limits. Below is a fully precise open problem with 21 concrete instances. Your task: **\*\*completely resolve at least one instance\*\*** — either by a rigorous proof or by an explicit, exactly verifiable counterexample. You choose which instance and which direction; both outcomes are equally valuable. Partial progress is welcome as a secondary output, but the goal is one full resolution.

**## 1. Definitions (all standard, stated to fix conventions)**

A **\*\*graphon\*\*** is a symmetric Lebesgue-measurable function $W:[0,1]^2\to[0,1]$. For a finite simple graph $H$ with vertex set $V(H)$ and edge set $E(H)$, the **\*\*homomorphism density\*\*** is

$$

 t(H,W) \\;=\\; \int\_{[0,1]^{V(H)}} \prod\_{uv\in E(H)} W(x\_u,x\_v)\\; \prod\_{u\in V(H)} dx\_u .

$$

(Maps are not required to be injective.) The **\*\*edge density\*\*** of $W$ is $p := t(K\_2,W) = \iint W$.

For a graph $H$ with chromatic polynomial $\chi\_H$ and $v = v(H)$ vertices, define for $0\le p<1$

$$

 \Phi\_H(p) \\;:=\\; (1-p)^{v}\\,\chi\_H\\!\left(\frac{1}{1-p}\right),

 \qquad \Phi\_H(1):=1 \ \text{(continuous extension)}.

$$

This is a polynomial in $p$ with integer coefficients (expanded forms are given below for each instance).

**\*\*Conjectured inequality for a given $H$\*\*** (this is the object to prove or disprove):

\> For every graphon $W$ with edge density $p = t(K\_2,W) \ge 1 - \dfrac{1}{\chi(H)-1}$, it holds that $t(H,W)\ \ge\ \Phi\_H(p)$.

Here $\chi(H)$ is the chromatic number. The density restriction is essential: below the threshold the inequality is generally false and is not conjectured.

Equivalent finite form: since finite graphs are dense in the graphon space and both sides are continuous in the relevant densities, the statement for $H$ is equivalent to: for every finite simple graph $G$ (with $t(F,G) := \hom(F,G)/n^{v(F)}$, so $t(K\_2,G)=2e(G)/n^2$), $t(K\_2,G)\ge$ threshold implies $t(H,G)\ge\Phi\_H(t(K\_2,G))$. You may work in either setting. For a **\*\*counterexample\*\*** you may restrict to step graphons without loss of generality: if $W$ is a step function with $k$ parts of measures $\alpha\_1,\dots,\alpha\_k$ ($\sum\alpha\_i=1$) and symmetric value matrix $M\in[0,1]^{k\times k}$, then

$$

 t(H,W) = \sum\_{\varphi\:V(H)\to[k]}\ \prod\_{uv\in E(H)} M\_{\varphi(u)\varphi(v)}\ \prod\_{u\in V(H)}\alpha\_{\varphi(u)} .

$$

**## 2. Hard constraints any answer must respect**

**\*\*(a) Infinitely many equality cases.\*\*** Let $T\_k$ denote the balanced Turán graphon ($k$ equal parts, $W=0$ on the $k$ diagonal blocks, $W=1$ off-diagonal), with $p = 1-1/k$. Then $t(H,T\_k)=\chi\_H(k)/k^{v(H)}$ and $\Phi\_H(1-1/k)=\chi\_H(k)/k^{v(H)}$ — **\*\*equality holds at $T\_k$ for every $k \ge \chi(H)-1$\*\***, and also at $W\equiv 1$. A proof cannot afford any loss at these points; a counterexample must do strictly better than all of them.

**\*\*(b) The inequality is false for some $H$.\*\*** Among all 117 non-bipartite graphs on $\le 6$ vertices (no isolated vertices, no isolated-edge components), 23 have exact counterexamples and 73 have accepted proofs; the 21 below are exactly the unresolved ones. Known counterexamples come in two shapes: (i) tensor products $W = T\_{k\_1}\otimes\cdots\otimes T\_{k\_s}$ (for which $p=\prod\_i(1-1/k\_i)$ and $t(H,W)=\prod\_i \chi\_H(k\_i)/k\_i^{v(H)}$), and (ii) local perturbations of $T\_2$ or $T\_3$, including one genuinely 5-step "fractional-fibre" perturbation of $T\_2$ at $p\approx 1/2$. So no general theorem is possible; the structure of the specific $H$ must be used.

**\*\*(c) What has already been ruled out for all 21 instances below.\*\*** Do not spend effort re-deriving these:

\- **\*\*Tensor counterexamples are exhausted\*\***: all $T\_{k\_1}\otimes T\_{k\_2}$ with $k\_i\le 500$, repeated and consecutive products with endpoints $\le 1000$, and $2\times10^6$ random products of lengths 2–24 with factors $\le 5000$ were checked in exact arithmetic. None violates the inequality for these 21 graphs.

\- **\*\*Local stability holds\*\***: for each of the 21 graphs there is a proven explicit $L^\infty$-radius around every interior Turán graphon $T\_k$, $k\ge\chi(H)$, and around the critical threshold Turán graphon, inside which the inequality holds. So a counterexample cannot be an $L^\infty$-small perturbation of any balanced Turán graphon. (Perturbations of small measure but order-one amplitude are *\*not\** excluded in general — that is how the one known non-tensor 6-vertex counterexample works.)

\- **\*\*The high-density endpoint is closed\*\***: for each of the 21 graphs there is a proven explicit $\varepsilon\_H>0$ such that the inequality holds for **\*\*every\*\*** graphon with $1-p\le\varepsilon\_H$. (The proven radii are small, e.g. of order $10^{-6}$ to $10^{-12}$.) So a counterexample must live at "middle" densities; a proof, however, should ideally cover the whole range on its own.

\- **\*\*The constant graphon is safe\*\***: $W\equiv p$ satisfies the inequality strictly in the open range for all 21 graphs.

**\*\*(d) Rigor standard.\*\*** A proof must be complete and self-contained modulo the citable literature (e.g. Goodman's bound, Moon–Moser clique-density inequalities $t\_{j}\ge t\_{j-1}\bigl(1-(j-1)(1-p)\bigr)$, Kruskal–Katona, Reiher's clique density theorem, standard entropy/Cauchy–Schwarz/Hölder arguments, Lovász's graph-limits book). Numerical SDP/flag-algebra output is acceptable **\*\*only\*\*** if rounded to an exact rational certificate that can be verified by hand or exact arithmetic. A counterexample must be an explicit step graphon with rational part sizes and rational values, an explicit rational $p$ in the admissible range, and an exact rational evaluation of both $t(H,W)$ and $\Phi\_H(p)$ exhibiting $t(H,W)<\Phi\_H(p)$.

Vertices are labeled $0,\dots,v-1$. "Threshold" is $1-1/(\chi(H)-1)$; the inequality is claimed exactly on $p\in[\text{threshold},1]$. **# Three open homomorphism-density inequalities**

You are a research mathematician in extremal graph theory. Below are three concrete open problems. **\*\*Completely resolve at least one\*\*** — by rigorous proof or by an explicit, exactly verifiable counterexample. Both directions are valuable; pick the instance you judge most tractable.

**## Setup**

A graphon is a symmetric measurable $W:[0,1]^2\to[0,1]$; for a finite simple graph $H$,

$$

 t(H,W)=\int\_{[0,1]^{V(H)}}\prod\_{uv\in E(H)}W(x\_u,x\_v)\prod\_u dx\_u,

 \qquad p:=t(K\_2,W).

$$

For each $H$ below, the question is whether every graphon with $p\ge 1-\frac{1}{\chi(H)-1}$ satisfies

$$

 t(H,W)\ \ge\ \Phi\_H(p):=(1-p)^{v(H)}\\,\chi\_H\\!\left(\tfrac{1}{1-p}\right),

$$

where $\chi\_H$ is the chromatic polynomial. Prove it on the full stated range, or give a counterexample.

**## The three instances**

**\*\*Problem A (main target).\*\*** $H$ = two vertex-disjoint triangles joined by one edge (a bridge): vertices $0..5$, edges $\\{01,02,12,\\;34,35,45,\\;03\\}$. Here $\chi\_H(x)=x(x-1)^3(x-2)^2$, and the claim reads

$$

 t(H,W)\ \ge\ p^3(2p-1)^2 \qquad\text{for } p\ge \tfrac12 .

$$

Equivalently, with the rooted-triangle density $\tau(x):=\iint W(x,a)W(x,b)W(a,b)\\,da\\,db$:

$$

 \iint W(x,y)\\,\tau(x)\\,\tau(y)\\,dx\\,dy\ \ge\ p^3(2p-1)^2 .

$$

Known: $\int\tau = t(K\_3,W)\ge p(2p-1)$ (Goodman), and an entropy argument gives $t(H,W)\ge[p(2p-1)]^{5/2}$, which is weaker. Naive Cauchy–Schwarz decouplings fail because they are not tight at the equality cases below.

**\*\*Problem B (smallest gap).\*\*** $H$ = $K\_4$ on $\\{0,2,3,4\\}$ with two triangles glued on edges: triangle $\\{0,4,5\\}$ on edge $\\{0,4\\}$ and triangle $\\{1,2,3\\}$ on edge $\\{2,3\\}$. Edges: $\\{02,03,04,05,12,13,23,24,34,45\\}$; $\chi\_H(x)=x(x-1)(x-2)^3(x-3)$. Claim:

$$

 t(H,W)\ \ge\ p(2p-1)^3(3p-2) \qquad\text{for } p\ge \tfrac23 .

$$

Known (entropy): $t(H,W)\ \ge\ p(2p-1)^2(3p-2)^2$. Since $3p-2\le 2p-1$ on the range, the entire gap is upgrading one factor $(3p-2)$ to $(2p-1)$.

**\*\*Problem C (smallest graph).\*\*** $H$ = the house: 5-cycle $0\\!-\\!1\\!-\\!2\\!-\\!3\\!-\\!4\\!-\\!0$ plus chord $\\{0,3\\}$ (a triangle and a 4-cycle glued along an edge). $\chi\_H(x)=x(x-1)(x-2)(x^2-3x+3)$. Claim:

$$

 t(H,W)\ \ge\ p(2p-1)(3p^2-3p+1) \qquad\text{for } p\ge \tfrac12 .

$$

**## Facts any answer must respect**

1\. **\*\*Equality cases.\*\*** For the balanced Turán graphon $T\_k$ ($k$ equal parts, $0$ on diagonal blocks, $1$ off-diagonal; $p=1-1/k$): $t(H,T\_k)=\chi\_H(k)/k^{v(H)}=\Phi\_H(1-1/k)$. So **\*\*equality holds at every $T\_k$ with $k\ge\chi(H)-1$\*\***, and at $W\equiv1$. A proof must be tight at all of them; a counterexample must beat all of them.

2\. **\*\*The inequality is false for some graphs\*\*** of the same size (exact counterexamples exist for 23 sibling graphs, via tensor products $T\_{k\_1}\otimes\cdots\otimes T\_{k\_s}$, where $t$ is multiplicative and $p=\prod(1-1/k\_i)$, or via local perturbations of $T\_2$/$T\_3$). So the specific structure of $H$ must be used.

3\. **\*\*Already ruled out for these three $H$\*\*** (do not redo): all tensor-product counterexamples up to very large search bounds; any $L^\infty$-small perturbation of any $T\_k$ (proven local stability); the near-complete regime ($1-p$ small, proven); the constant graphon $W\equiv p$ (satisfies the inequality strictly). A counterexample, if any, is non-tensor and at middle densities — e.g. a perturbation of $T\_2$ or $T\_3$ of small measure but order-one amplitude.

4\. **\*\*Verification standard.\*\*** A counterexample must be a step graphon: rational part sizes $\alpha\_i$, rational symmetric value matrix $M$, with

$$ t(H,W)=\sum\_{\varphi\:V(H)\to[k]}\prod\_{uv\in E(H)}M\_{\varphi(u)\varphi(v)}\prod\_u \alpha\_{\varphi(u)}, $$

and exact rational values showing $t(H,W)<\Phi\_H(p)$. A proof must be complete, with every step justified (standard results — Goodman, Moon–Moser, Kruskal–Katona, Reiher's clique density theorem, Cauchy–Schwarz/entropy — may be cited).

**## Output**

State which problem you resolve and in which direction, then give the full proof or the explicit certificate. If you cannot fully resolve one, give your best partial result with proven claims cleanly separated from heuristics.

Consider a house graph, which has 5 vertices and 6 edges, that is constructed by gluing triangle and 4-cycle by an edge. 

Our conjecture is that this graph satisfies the following homomorphism density lower bound:
t(H, W) >= chi_H(1 / (1-p)) (1-p)^{v(H)} whenever p >= 1 - 1 / (chi(H) - 1)
where chi_H is the chromatic polynomial of H, v(H) is number of vertices in H, chi(H) is the chromatic number of H, and p is the edge density of W, t(K_2, W). 

This conjecture emerges from the turan graph optimality, if this conjecture is true, then the balanced complete k-partite graphons are minimisers of H-density under edge density constraints p = 1 - 1 / k. 

Work until you prove or disprove this conjecture.

## Status

I did **not** obtain a complete proof or a counterexample. The conjecture survives the exact reductions, local analysis, and structured-family tests below, but the remaining mixed path-kernel inequality is genuinely nontrivial. Thus the conclusions below are rigorous partial results, not a proof of the full statement.

Let \(H\) be the house graph with vertices \(u,v,a,b,c\) and edges
\[
uv,\ ua,\ va,\ ub,\ bc,\ cv.
\]
Equivalently, \(H\) is the generalized theta graph \(\Theta(1,2,3)\), with three internally disjoint \(u\)-\(v\) paths of lengths \(1,2,3\).

## 1. The conjectured bound explicitly

Because \(H\) is obtained by gluing \(K_3\) and \(C_4\) along \(K_2\),
\[
\chi_H(x)
=\frac{\chi_{K_3}(x)\chi_{C_4}(x)}{\chi_{K_2}(x)}
=x(x-1)(x-2)(x^2-3x+3).
\]
Thus \(\chi(H)=3\), so the relevant range is \(p\ge \tfrac12\). Writing \(q=1-p\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
(1-p)^5\chi_H\!\left(\frac1{1-p}\right)
&=p(2p-1)(p^3+q^3)\\
&=6p^4-9p^3+5p^2-p.
\end{aligned}
\]
The conjecture is therefore
\[
\boxed{\quad
t(H,W)\ge p(2p-1)\bigl(p^3+(1-p)^3\bigr),
\qquad p\ge\frac12.
\quad}
\tag{1}
\]

The normalization is exactly the one forced by balanced multipartite graphons: if \(T_k\) is the balanced complete \(k\)-partite graphon, then
\[
t(F,T_k)=\frac{\chi_F(k)}{k^{v(F)}},
\qquad
t(K_2,T_k)=1-\frac1k.
\]
This is the general motivation used in the pure-chordal note. fileciteturn0file1

The house is **not** covered by the pure-chordal theorem: its four cycle vertices induce a chordless \(C_4\), and its maximal cliques do not all have the same size. The tensor-product obstruction for graphs of even girth also does not apply, since the house has girth \(3\). fileciteturn0file2

## 2. Sharpness at every Turán density

For \(p=1-\frac1k\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
t(H,T_k)
&=\frac{k(k-1)(k-2)(k^2-3k+3)}{k^5}\\
&=p(2p-1)(p^3+q^3).
\end{aligned}
\]
Hence equality in (1) holds at every balanced complete \(k\)-partite graphon.

This confirms that the proposed right-hand side is the correct Turán interpolation polynomial.

## 3. The exact path-kernel formulation

Let \(T=T_W\) be the graphon operator, and write \(T^j(x,y)\) for the kernel of its \(j\)-th power. Rooting the three \(u\)-\(v\) paths of lengths \(1,2,3\) gives
\[
\boxed{\quad
t(H,W)
=
\int_{[0,1]^2}
W(x,y)\,T^2(x,y)\,T^3(x,y)\,dx\,dy.
\quad}
\tag{2}
\]

This is the central analytic difficulty. The analogous individual quantities are
\[
t(K_3,W)=\int W(x,y)T^2(x,y)\,dx\,dy
\]
and
\[
t(C_4,W)=\int W(x,y)T^3(x,y)\,dx\,dy.
\]
A generic edge-amalgamation inequality such as
\[
t(H,W)\stackrel{?}{\ge}
\frac{t(K_3,W)t(C_4,W)}{p}
\]
would immediately be useful, but such a positive-correlation assertion is not valid for arbitrary rooted extension kernels. The pure-chordal entropy argument works because all bags are identical cliques and have compatible separator marginals; that compatibility is absent for a triangle and a \(4\)-cycle.

## 4. An exact reduction to the sharp \(C_5\) inequality

The house is also obtained by adding a distance-two chord to \(C_5\). Put \(U=1-W\). If the added chord joins \(x_0\) and \(x_2\), define
\[
L(W):=
\int_{[0,1]^5}
U(x_0,x_2)
\prod_{i=0}^{4}W(x_i,x_{i+1})\,
dx_0\cdots dx_4,
\qquad x_5=x_0.
\]
Then
\[
t(H,W)=t(C_5,W)-L(W).
\tag{3}
\]
Equivalently,
\[
L(W)=\int U(x,y)T_W^2(x,y)T_W^3(x,y)\,dx\,dy.
\]

The audited odd-cycle result gives
\[
t(C_5,W)\ge g_5(p):=p^5-pq^4.
\]
fileciteturn0file0

A direct calculation shows
\[
g_5(p)-p(2p-1)(p^3+q^3)
=p^2q(2p-1).
\tag{4}
\]
Consequently, the house conjecture is equivalent to the following sharp chord-loss inequality:
\[
\boxed{\quad
L(W)
\le
\bigl[t(C_5,W)-(p^5-pq^4)\bigr]
+p^2q(2p-1).
\quad}
\tag{5}
\]

This reduction is useful because both terms on the right are nonnegative. It is also sharp: at every \(T_k\), the \(C_5\) surplus in brackets vanishes and
\[
L(T_k)=p^2q(2p-1).
\]
Thus a proof based on the \(C_5\) theorem must retain the deletion/chord-loss term quantitatively; simply bounding \(L\) by deleting some of its factors loses the required sharpness.

## 5. Strict first-order local minimality of every \(T_k\)

The balanced Turán graphon is not merely an equality example. It is a strict first-order local minimizer of the house density under the edge-density constraint.

For an edge \(e\in E(H)\), the chromatic polynomial of \(H/e\) depends on the position of \(e\). The relevant polynomials are

\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c}
\text{edge type}&\text{multiplicity}&\chi_{H/e}(x)\\ \hline
\text{shared triangle--square edge}&1&
x^4-4x^3+5x^2-2x\\
\text{other triangle edges}&2&
x^4-4x^3+6x^2-3x\\
\text{three remaining square edges}&3&
x^4-5x^3+8x^2-4x .
\end{array}
\]

Let \(F\) be a nonzero admissible first-order perturbation of \(T_k\) preserving edge density. Since \(T_k\) is \(0\)-\(1\)-valued, \(F\ge0\) on the within-part blocks and \(F\le0\) on the cross-part blocks. Put
\[
A_{\mathrm{in}}
=
\int_{\{\text{within the same part}\}}F.
\]
The edge constraint gives \(A_{\mathrm{out}}=-A_{\mathrm{in}}\), and \(A_{\mathrm{in}}>0\).

The first-variation kernel is constant on within-part blocks and on cross-part blocks. Its difference is
\[
K_{\mathrm{in}}-K_{\mathrm{out}}
=
\frac{
\displaystyle
\sum_{e\in E(H)}\chi_{H/e}(k)
-\frac{6}{k-1}\chi_H(k)
}{k^4}.
\]
Using the displayed contraction polynomials,
\[
\sum_{e\in E(H)}\chi_{H/e}(k)
-\frac{6}{k-1}\chi_H(k)
=
k(3k^2-13k+16).
\]
Therefore
\[
\delta t(H,T_k)[F]
=
\frac{3k^2-13k+16}{k^3}\,A_{\mathrm{in}}.
\]
Since
\[
3k^2-13k+16>0
\]
for every real \(k\) — its discriminant is \(169-192=-23\) — we obtain
\[
\boxed{\quad
\delta t(H,T_k)[F]>0
\quad}
\]
for every nonzero edge-preserving admissible direction.

Thus every \(T_k\) is a strict first-order local minimizer. This rules out all infinitesimal counterexamples around the proposed equality graphons, although it does not establish global minimality.

## 6. Exact verification on the natural near-bipartite family

Partition \([0,1]\) into two sets \(A,B\) of measure \(1/2\), and define
\[
W_r(x,y)=
\begin{cases}
1,&x\in A,\ y\in B\ \text{or conversely},\\
r,&x,y\in A\ \text{or}\ x,y\in B,
\end{cases}
\qquad 0\le r\le1.
\]
Its edge density is
\[
p=\frac{1+r}{2},
\qquad r=2p-1,
\]
and it is \(p\)-regular.

A direct enumeration of the \(2^5\) assignments of the house vertices to \(A,B\) gives
\[
t(H,W_r)
=
\frac{4r+6r^2+12r^3+8r^4+2r^6}{32}.
\]
In terms of \(p\) and \(q=1-p\), this is
\[
t(H,W_r)
=
p^6-p^3q^3+p^2q^4-pq^5.
\]
Subtracting the conjectured bound gives the exact factorization
\[
\boxed{\quad
t(H,W_r)-p(2p-1)(p^3+q^3)
=
p^2q^2(2p-1)^2
\ge0.
\quad}
\tag{6}
\]

Hence the conjecture holds on the equal-half near-bipartite family, with a quartically small margin near \(p=\frac12\). This is relevant because near-bipartite graphons are the most natural potential competitors close to the Mantel threshold.

The constant graphon \(W\equiv p\) is also safe:
\[
t(H,W)=p^6,
\]
and
\[

### 1.2 The \(C_5\) reduction gives exactly the same correction

Write \(K_j^W(x,y)\) for the rooted \(j\)-edge path kernel, so that

\]

It is also a \(C_5\) with a distance-two chord. Therefore, with \(U=1-W\), define

\int U(x,y)K_2^W(x,y)K_3^W(x,y)\,dx\,dy.
\tag{5}
\]

\tag{6}
\]

A direct calculation gives

g_5(p)-prc=p^2qr.

Then
\[

\tag{8}

where
\[
\Gamma_5(W)=x_4-c_5
=
\int W(x_0,x_4)\prod_{i=0}^{3}U(x_i,x_{i+1})\,dx_0\cdots dx_4

={}&4\|Tg\|_2^2+(8q-5)\langle g,Tg\rangle

={}&4\left\|Tg+\frac{8q-5}{8}g\right\|_2^2

=

## 2. Exact reduction for regular graphons

There is a cleaner form of the problem when \(W\) is \(p\)-regular. Then \(U=1-W\) is \(q\)-regular. On the decomposition
\[
L^2([0,1])=\mathbb R1\oplus1^\perp
\]
we may write
\[
T_W=pJ-A,\qquad T_U=qJ+A,
\tag{13}
\]
where \(Jf=\langle f,1\rangle1\) and \(JA=AJ=0\).

It follows immediately that
\[
T_W^2-T_U^2=(p^2-q^2)J=rJ
\tag{14}
\]
and, since the third power is odd,
\[
T_W^3+T_U^3=(p^3+q^3)J=cJ.
\tag{15}
\]

Using (14)–(15) in (4) gives an exact identity. First,
\[
\begin{aligned}
t(H,W)
&=\int W K_2^W(c-K_3^U)\\
&=c\,t(K_3,W)
 -r\int W K_3^U
 -\int W K_2^U K_3^U.
\end{aligned}
\]
Regularity gives
\[
\int W K_3^U=q^3-t(C_4,U)
\tag{16}
\]
and
\[
\int W K_2^U K_3^U=t(C_5,U)-t(H,U).
\tag{17}
\]
Moreover,
\[
t(K_3,W)+t(K_3,U)=p^3+q^3=c.
\tag{18}
\]

Subtracting the target \(prc\), and using \(c-pr=q^2\), gives
\[
\boxed{
\begin{aligned}
t(H,W)-prc
={}&c\bigl(q^2-t(C_3,U)\bigr)
-r\bigl(q^3-t(C_4,U)\bigr)\\
&\quad-t(C_5,U)+t(H,U).
\end{aligned}}
\tag{19}
\]

This identity contains only cycle densities and the house density in the complement.

## 3. Markov-kernel form

Assume \(q>0\) and normalize
\[
U=qP.
\]
Then \(P\) is a symmetric Markov kernel:
\[
P\ge0,\qquad \int P(x,y)\,dy=1.
\]
Write
\[
\tau_j=t(C_j,P),\qquad \Theta=t(H,P).
\]
Since the house has six edges, (19) becomes
\[
\boxed{
\frac{t(H,W)-prc}{q^2}
=
c(1-q\tau_3)
-rq(1-q\tau_4)
-q^3\tau_5
+q^4\Theta.
}
\tag{20}
\]

Thus the regular case is reduced to the following completely explicit Markov-kernel inequality:
\[
\boxed{
c(1-q\tau_3)
-rq(1-q\tau_4)
-q^3\tau_5
+q^4\Theta\ge0.
}
\tag{21}
\]

No graph flags occur in (21).

## 4. A correlation inequality that would substantially close the regular case

The computational evidence points consistently to
\[
\boxed{
\Theta\ge \tau_3\tau_5
}
\tag{22}
\]
for every symmetric Markov kernel \(P\).

This is precisely
\[
t\!\left(C_3\mathbin{\cup_{P_2}}C_5,P\right)
\ge
t(C_3,P)t(C_5,P),
\tag{23}
\]
because \(t(P_2,P)=1\).

There is a useful two-stage formulation of (22). For \(a\in[0,1]\), let
\[
r_a(x)=P(a,x).
\]
Then
\[
\Theta
=
\int_a\int_{x,y}
r_a(x)r_a(y)P(x,y)P^3(x,y)\,dx\,dy\,da,
\tag{24}
\]
while
\[
P^3(a,a)
=
\int r_a(x)r_a(y)P(x,y)\,dx\,dy
\tag{25}
\]
and
\[
P^5(a,a)
=
\int r_a(x)r_a(y)P^3(x,y)\,dx\,dy.
\tag{26}
\]

Therefore (22) would follow from the two inequalities
\[
\int r(x)r(y)P(x,y)P^3(x,y)\,dx\,dy
\ge
\left(\int rrP\right)\left(\int rrP^3\right)
\tag{27}
\]
for every probability density \(r\), and
\[
\int P^3(a,a)P^5(a,a)\,da
\ge
\tau_3\tau_5.
\tag{28}
\]

I tested (27), (28), and (22) on large collections of finite symmetric Markov kernels, including convex combinations of symmetric permutation kernels, dense random kernels, nearly reducible kernels, and kernels with substantial negative spectrum. No violation was found. This is evidence only, not a proof.

A notable diagnostic is that the more general covariance
\[
\int rr\,P^aP^b
-
\left(\int rrP^a\right)\left(\int rrP^b\right)
\tag{29}
\]
appears nonnegative when \(a\) and \(b\) have the same parity, but can be negative when their parities differ. Thus (27) seems to be using a genuine parity-sensitive Markov correlation, rather than a generic positive-association assertion.

## 5. Spectral reduction after the correlation inequality

Suppose (22) is established. Let
\[
1,\lambda_1,\lambda_2,\ldots
\]
be the spectrum of \(T_P\), where \(1\) is the principal eigenvalue, and set
\[
s_j=\sum_{i\ge1}\lambda_i^j.
\]
Then
\[
\tau_j=1+s_j.
\]
Substituting \(\Theta\ge\tau_3\tau_5\) into (20), the required inequality follows from
\[
\boxed{
(p^3-q^3s_5)(p-qs_3)
\ge
rq(p-qs_4).
}
\tag{30}
\]

There is an elementary proof of (30) in the high-density range \(p\ge2/3\). Since
\[
\int U^2\le\int U=q,
\]
we have
\[
q(1+s_2)\le1.
\]
Put
\[
\delta=\frac pq-s_2\ge0
\]
and
\[
A_3=\sum_i\lambda_i^2(1-\lambda_i),\qquad
A_4=\sum_i\lambda_i^2(1-\lambda_i^2),\qquad
A_5=\sum_i\lambda_i^2(1-\lambda_i^3).
\]
Then
\[
p-qs_3=q(\delta+A_3),
\qquad
p-qs_4=q(\delta+A_4),
\tag{31}
\]
and
\[
p^3-q^3s_5=pr+q^3(\delta+A_5).
\tag{32}
\]
For every \(\lambda\in[-1,1]\),
\[
\lambda^2(1-\lambda^2)
=
(1+\lambda)\lambda^2(1-\lambda)
\le
2\lambda^2(1-\lambda),
\]
so
\[
\delta+A_4\le2(\delta+A_3).
\tag{33}
\]
After dividing (30) by \(q\), its left side minus its right side is at least
\[
\begin{aligned}
pr(\delta+A_3)-rq(\delta+A_4)
&\ge
pr(\delta+A_3)-2rq(\delta+A_3)\\
&=
r(p-2q)(\delta+A_3).
\end{aligned}
\]
This is nonnegative whenever \(p\ge2q\), equivalently \(p\ge2/3\).

Hence:

> **Conditional regular theorem.** If the Markov correlation inequality (22) holds, then the house conjecture holds for every \(p\)-regular graphon in the range \(p\ge2/3\).

For \(1/2\le p\le2/3\), the crude estimate \(A_4\le2A_3\) is insufficient, and the full Markov constraints must be used.

## 6. Why a spectral Bernstein certificate alone is not enough

It is tempting to treat the \(\lambda_i\) merely as numbers satisfying
\[
-1\le\lambda_i\le1,
\qquad
q(1+s_2)\le1,
\]
and prove (30) by Bernstein subdivision. That relaxation is too large: artificial spectral sequences satisfying these conditions can violate (30). Such sequences need not be spectra of an entrywise nonnegative Markov kernel.

Therefore a successful computational certificate must retain at least one of:

1. the correlation term \(\Theta-\tau_3\tau_5\);
2. entrywise nonnegativity of the Markov kernel;
3. the coupling between eigenvalues and eigenfunctions;
4. in the general irregular case, the deletion term \(\Gamma_5\) in (11).

A Bernstein certificate over only \((q,s_2,s_3,s_4,s_5)\) is unlikely to be valid.

\[

be the rooted two-edge path kernel, and define
\[

D(x,y):=(1-W(x,y))C(x,y).
\]
Thus
\[
A+D=C.
\]

Consider a \(5\)-cycle in the form
\[
y-a-x-b-z-y.
\]
The two distance-two chords incident to \(x\) are \(xy\) and \(xz\). Define
\[
\begin{aligned}
F&:=\int W(y,z)A(x,y)A(x,z)\,dx\,dy\,dz,\\
R&:=\int W(y,z)A(x,y)D(x,z)\,dx\,dy\,dz,\\
G&:=\int W(y,z)D(x,y)D(x,z)\,dx\,dy\,dz.
\end{aligned}
\tag{2}
\]
By symmetry, the density with \(D(x,y)A(x,z)\) is also \(R\).

Expanding \(C=A+D\) gives
\[
t(C_5,W)=F+2R+G.
\tag{3}
\]
On the other hand, imposing the chord \(xy\) produces the house, so
\[
t(H,W)=F+R.
\tag{4}
\]
Therefore
\[
\boxed{\;
2t(H,W)=F+t(C_5,W)-G.
\;}
\tag{5}
\]

The interpretation is useful:

- \(F\) is the density where both distance-two chords are present;
- \(G\) is the density where both are absent;
- the two mixed cases are the two symmetric realizations of the house.

K(x,y):=U(x,y)C_U(x,y).

D=rU+K.
\tag{28}

For nonnegative kernels \(K_1,K_2\), put

=
\int W(y,z)K_1(x,y)K_2(x,z)\,dx\,dy\,dz.

Since \(U\) is \(q\)-regular,
\[
C_U(x,y)\le q,
\]
and therefore
\[
K\le qU,\qquad K\le C_U.
\]
It follows that
\[
\begin{aligned}
G
&=\mathcal Q(rU+K,rU+K)\\
&=r^2n+2r\mathcal Q(U,K)+\mathcal Q(K,K)\\
&\le r^2n+2rq\,n+\Gamma_5\\
&=\Gamma_5+r n.
\end{aligned}
\tag{29}
\]
Here we used
\[
r^2+2rq=r(r+2q)=r.

Substituting this into (23),
\[
\begin{aligned}
2\bigl(t(H,W)-B(p)\bigr)
&\ge
(3r^2-r)n
+\frac{3r}{p}n^2
+\frac{n^3}{p^2}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{30}

Hence this is nonnegative whenever \(3r\ge1\), namely \(p\ge2/3\).

## 2. A sharper general estimate on \(G\)

The previous estimate was only \(G\le n\). There is a more informative degree-sensitive bound.

For fixed \(x\), put
\[
n_x
=
\int W(y,z)U(x,y)U(x,z)\,dy\,dz.
\tag{8}
\]
Then
\[
n=\int n_x\,dx,
\qquad 0\le n_x\le1.
\]

Since a common \(W\)-neighbour of \(x\) and \(y\) is, in particular, a \(W\)-neighbour of \(x\),
\[
C_W(x,y)\le d_W(x)=p-g(x).
\]
The same estimate applies to \(C_W(x,z)\). Consequently,
\[
G
\le
\int (p-g(x))^2n_x\,dx.
\tag{9}
\]

By the triangle inequality in the weighted \(L^2\)-space \(n_xdx\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
\left(\int (p-g)^2n_x\right)^{1/2}
&\le
p\left(\int n_x\right)^{1/2}
+
\left(\int g^2n_x\right)^{1/2}\\
&\le p\sqrt n+\sqrt v.
\end{aligned}
\]
Therefore
\[
\boxed{
G\le
\min\left\{n,\,(p\sqrt n+\sqrt v)^2\right\}.
}
\tag{10}
\]

Combining (2)–(7) and \(a=pr+\delta\) gives the fully explicit certificate
\[
\boxed{
\begin{aligned}
2\bigl(t(H,W)-B(p)\bigr)
\ge{}&
3r^2\delta
+\frac{3r}{p}\delta^2
+\frac{\delta^3}{p^2}\\
&+\kappa(q)v+\Gamma\\
&-\min\left\{n,\,(p\sqrt n+\sqrt v)^2\right\},
\end{aligned}}
\tag{11}
\]
where
\[
\delta=2v+n.
\]

This is rigorous for every graphon. Its significance is that degree irregularity is now quantitatively expensive:

- the obstruction \(G\) grows at most as \((p\sqrt n+\sqrt v)^2\);
- the triangle-tree surplus already contains \(6r^2v\);
- the \(C_5\) certificate contributes the additional coercive term \(\kappa(q)v\).

Thus any counterexample in the remaining density interval would have to be close to regular in the precise sense that \(v\) is small relative to \(n\). The genuinely difficult boundary is therefore the degree-regular one, not highly irregular graphons.

## 3. An exact identity for regular graphons

Now suppose \(W\) is \(p\)-regular. Then \(U\) is \(q\)-regular, so
\[
g=0,\qquad v=0,\qquad \Phi_5=0,\qquad \delta=n.
\]
Moreover,
\[
C_W=r+C_U.
\tag{12}
\]

Write \(C=C_U\), and introduce
\[
\begin{aligned}
P&:=Q(W,WC),\\
L&:=Q(U,UC),\\
M&:=
\int W(y,z)W(x,y)C(x,y)C(x,z)\,dx\,dy\,dz.
\end{aligned}
\tag{13}
\]

Expanding \(F\) using \(C_W=r+C\) gives
\[
F
=
pr^3+r^2n+2rP+Q(WC,WC).
\tag{14}
\]
Similarly,
\[
G
=
r^2n+2rL+Q(UC,UC).
\tag{15}
\]

There is also the exact pointwise algebra
\[
\begin{aligned}
&Q(WC,WC)+\Gamma-Q(UC,UC)\\
&\quad=
\int W(y,z)
\bigl[W(x,y)W(x,z)+1-U(x,y)U(x,z)\bigr]
C(x,y)C(x,z)\\
&\quad=
\int W(y,z)\bigl[W(x,y)+W(x,z)\bigr]
C(x,y)C(x,z)\\
&\quad=2M.
\end{aligned}
\tag{16}
\]
Substituting (14)–(16) into (7) produces:

\[
\boxed{
t(H,W)-B(p)=M+r(P-L).
}
\tag{17}
\]

Expanding \(P-L\) gives an especially compact form:

\[
\boxed{
\begin{aligned}
t(H,W)-B(p)
={}&
\int W(y,z)C_U(x,z)\\
&\quad\cdot
\Bigl[
W(x,y)C_U(x,y)
+r\bigl(W(x,y)+W(x,z)-1\bigr)
\Bigr]
\,dx\,dy\,dz.
\end{aligned}}
\tag{18}
\]

This identity is exact. It contains only three integration variables and the two-step complement kernel.

The symmetric version is
\[
\boxed{
\begin{aligned}
t(H,W)-B(p)
=\frac12\int W(y,z)\Bigl[
& C_U(x,y)C_U(x,z)
   \bigl(W(x,y)+W(x,z)\bigr)\\
&+r\bigl(C_U(x,y)+C_U(x,z)\bigr)
   \bigl(W(x,y)+W(x,z)-1\bigr)
\Bigr].
\end{aligned}}
\tag{19}
\]

At \(p=\frac12\), \(r=0\), and (18) is manifestly nonnegative. At every balanced Turán graphon, its integrand integrates to zero exactly. Hence no slack has been introduced.

The regular case is now equivalent to the single inequality
\[
\boxed{
M\ge r(L-P).
}
\tag{20}
\]

The term \(P-L\) can be negative; consequently, it is not enough to prove \(P\ge L\), and that inequality is in fact false on general regular step graphons. The compensation by \(M\) is essential.

A particularly clean strengthening emerged:

t(H,W)\stackrel{?}{\ge}
p(2p-1)
\bigl[t(K_3,W)+t(K_3,1-W)\bigr].

=
1-3p+3\int d_W(x)^2\,dx

p^3+q^3+3v.

Therefore (21) would give
\[

\ge
B(p)+3prv
\ge B(p).

This strengthening is exact at all balanced Turán graphons and is strictly stronger whenever the degree function is nonconstant. Finite-step numerical minimization has not produced a violation, including searches specifically directed at minimizing its defect. That is evidence only.

2\Bigl(
t(H,W)-pr\bigl[t(K_3,W)+t(K_3,U)\bigr]
\Bigr)
={}&
F-pr^3+\Gamma-G+\Psi,
\end{aligned}
\tag{23}

where

4\|T_Ug\|_2^2
+(8q-5)\langle g,T_Ug\rangle
+(3q-1)\|g\|_2^2.

\tag{24}

The quadratic form \(\Psi\) is not by itself nonnegative over the entire range, so a proof must couple it with \(F-pr^3\) and \(\Gamma-G\). This rules out a naive standalone operator-square argument.

# 2. Improved theorem for arbitrary graphons

For fixed \(x\), put
\[
n_x=\int W(y,z)U(x,y)U(x,z)\,dy\,dz.
\]
Then
\[
\int n_x\,dx=n.
\]

Since
\[
C_W(x,y)\le d_W(x)=p-g(x),
\]
we have
\[
G\le \int (p-g(x))^2n_x\,dx.
\]
Applying the triangle inequality in the weighted space \(L^2(n_xdx)\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
\sqrt G
&\le
p\left(\int n_x\right)^{1/2}
+
\left(\int g(x)^2n_x\,dx\right)^{1/2}\\
&\le p\sqrt n+\sqrt v,
\end{aligned}
\]
because \(0\le n_x\le1\). Therefore
\[
\boxed{G\le(p\sqrt n+\sqrt v)^2.}
\tag{10}
\]

\[
\begin{aligned}
2\bigl(t(H,W)-B(p)\bigr)
\ge{}&
3r^2(2v+n)
+\frac{3r}{p}(2v+n)^2
+\frac{(2v+n)^3}{p^2}\\
&+\kappa(q)v
-(p\sqrt n+\sqrt v)^2.
\end{aligned}
\tag{11}
\]

\[
x=\sqrt n,\qquad y=\sqrt v.
\]
The degree-two part of the right side of (11) is
\[
A(p)x^2-2pxy+C(p)y^2,
\tag{12}
\]
where
\[
A(p)=3r^2-p^2=11p^2-12p+3
\tag{13}
\]
and
\[
C(p)=6r^2+\kappa(q)-1
=
32p^2-30p+\frac{103}{16}.
\tag{14}
\]

\[
A(p)C(p)-p^2
=
\frac{Q(p)}{16},
\tag{15}

where
\[
Q(p)
=
5632p^4-11424p^3+8413p^2-2676p+309.
\tag{16}

p_0=0.766057528541100\ldots .

# 3. A full-interval theorem for regular graphons with bounded complement

There is a different reduction that works down to \(p=\frac12\).

Suppose that \(W\) is \(p\)-regular and that
\[
U=1-W\le 2q\qquad\text{a.e.}
\tag{18}
\]
Put
\[
s=2p-1.
\]
Since \(2q=1-s\), define
\[
V:=1-\frac{U}{1-s}
=\frac{W-s}{1-s}.
\tag{19}
\]
Condition (18) ensures that \(0\le V\le1\). Moreover,
\[
W=s+(1-s)V.
\tag{20}
\]

Because \(W\) is \(p\)-regular,
\[
d_V(x)
=
\frac{p-s}{1-s}
=
\frac12.
\]
Thus \(V\) is a \(1/2\)-regular graphon.

Write
\[
a=t(C_3,V),\qquad c_j=t(C_j,V),\qquad h=t(H,V).
\]

Expanding the six edges of \(H\) in (20), and integrating all leaves using \(d_V\equiv1/2\), gives the exact identity
\[
\boxed{
t(H,W)
=
C_0(s)+A(s)a+B_4(s)c_4+B_5(s)c_5+(1-s)^6h,
}
\tag{21}
\]
where
\[
C_0(s)
=
\frac{s^2(s^4-2s^3+12s^2-6s+11)}{16},
\tag{22}
\]
\[
A(s)=\frac{s(1-s)^3(s^2+3)}4,
\tag{23}
\]
\[
B_4(s)=s(1-s)^4,
\qquad
B_5(s)=s(1-s)^5.
\tag{24}
\]

The key spectral estimate is:

> **Lemma.** If \(V\) is \(1/2\)-regular, then
> \[
> \frac34t(C_3,V)+t(C_4,V)+t(C_5,V)\ge\frac18.
> \tag{25}
> \]

Indeed, write the spectrum of \(T_V\) as
\[
\frac12,\lambda_1,\lambda_2,\ldots .
\]
Every nonprincipal eigenvalue belongs to \([-1/2,1/2]\), and
\[
\sum_i\lambda_i^2
\le
\int V^2-\frac14
\le\frac14.
\]
For \(\lambda\in[-1/2,1/2]\),
\[
\frac34\lambda^3+\lambda^4+\lambda^5
\ge-\frac14\lambda^2.
\tag{26}
\]
For negative \(\lambda=-x\), this is exactly
\[
\frac14-\frac34x+x^2-x^3
=
\frac{(1-2x)(2x^2-x+1)}4
\ge0.
\]
The principal eigenvalue contributes
\[
\frac34\left(\frac12\right)^3
+\left(\frac12\right)^4
+\left(\frac12\right)^5
=
\frac3{16},
\]
while all remaining eigenvalues contribute at least \(-1/16\). This proves (25).

Now observe that
\[
A(s)-\frac34B_5(s)
=
\frac{s^2(3-s)(1-s)^3}{2}\ge0
\tag{27}
\]
and
\[
B_4(s)-B_5(s)=s^2(1-s)^4\ge0.
\tag{28}
\]
Consequently,
\[
\begin{aligned}
A(s)a+B_4(s)c_4+B_5(s)c_5
={}&
B_5(s)\left(\frac34a+c_4+c_5\right)\\
&+\left(A(s)-\frac34B_5(s)\right)a\\
&+\left(B_4(s)-B_5(s)\right)c_4\\
\ge{}&
\frac{B_5(s)}8+\frac{B_4(s)-B_5(s)}{16},
\end{aligned}
\tag{29}
\]
where we also used
\[
c_4\ge \left(t(K_2,V)\right)^4=\frac1{16}.
\]

Since
\[
B\!\left(\frac{1+s}{2}\right)
=
\frac{s(s+1)(3s^2+1)}8,
\]
a direct simplification gives
\[
C_0(s)+\frac{B_5(s)}8
+\frac{B_4(s)-B_5(s)}{16}
-
B\!\left(\frac{1+s}{2}\right)
=
\frac{s^3(1-s)^2}{4}.
\tag{30}
\]
Therefore
\[
t(H,W)-B(p)\ge\frac{s^3(1-s)^2}{4}\ge0.
\]

We have proved:

> **Theorem 2.** Let \(W\) be a \(p\)-regular graphon, \(p\ge\frac12\). If
> \[
> 1-W(x,y)\le2(1-p)\qquad\text{a.e.},
> \]
> then
> \[
> t(H,W)\ge p(2p-1)\bigl(p^3+(1-p)^3\bigr).
> \]

In particular, this covers the entire equal-half near-bipartite family, not merely \(p\ge2/3\).

\[
V=\frac{W-s}{1-s}
\]
is then a graphon of edge density \(1/2\), although it need not be regular.

For an arbitrary edge-\(1/2\) graphon, a spectral argument gives the following coefficient-tailored inequality. Put
\[
\alpha=s^3(1-s)^3,\qquad
\beta=s^2(1-s)^4,\qquad
\gamma=s(1-s)^5.
\]
Then
\[
\boxed{
\alpha t(C_3,V)+\beta t(C_4,V)+\gamma t(C_5,V)
\ge\frac{\beta}{8}.
}
\tag{32}
\]

To see this, let \(\lambda_1\ge\lambda_2\ge\cdots\) be the spectrum of \(T_V\). Since \(t(K_2,V)=1/2\),
\[
\lambda_1\ge\frac12,\qquad
\sum_i\lambda_i^2\le\frac12,
\qquad
\lambda_i\ge-\frac12.
\]
For \(x\in[0,1/2]\), the polynomial
\[
\alpha x-\beta x^2+\gamma x^3
\]
is increasing: its derivative has discriminant
\[
4\beta^2-12\alpha\gamma
=
-8s^4(1-s)^8\le0.
\]
Thus every negative eigenvalue contributes at least
\[
-\left(\frac{\alpha}{2}-\frac{\beta}{4}+\frac{\gamma}{8}\right)\lambda_i^2.
\]
Combining this with the principal eigenvalue and
\[
\sum_{\lambda_i<0}\lambda_i^2\le\frac12-\lambda_1^2
\]
gives (32); at \(\lambda_1=1/2\), the remaining expression is exactly \(\beta/8\).

Now expand
\[
t(H,s+(1-s)V)
=
\sum_{F\subseteq E(H)}
s^{6-e(F)}(1-s)^{e(F)}t(F,V).
\tag{33}
\]
Every bipartite subgraph occurring here is either a forest or a \(C_4\) with trees attached, so its density is at least \(2^{-e(F)}\). Retain the bare \(C_3,C_4,C_5\) terms and discard the other nonbipartite terms.

The resulting bipartite contribution is
\[
B_{\mathrm{bip}}(s)
=
\frac{s(s+1)(3s^3-s^2+5s+1)}{16}.
\tag{34}
\]
Using (32),
\[
t(H,W)\ge B_{\mathrm{bip}}(s)+\frac{\beta}{8}.
\]
Subtracting the target gives
\[
\boxed{
t(H,W)-B(p)
\ge
\frac{s(1-s)^2(2s^3-s^2+4s-1)}{16}.
}
\tag{35}
\]

Let \(s_*\) be the unique root in \((0,1)\) of
\[
2s^3-s^2+4s-1=0.
\]
Numerically,
\[
s_*=0.258055872478473\ldots ,
\]
and hence
\[
p_*=\frac{1+s_*}{2}
=0.629027936239236\ldots .
\]

Therefore:

> **Theorem 3.** If
> \[
> W(x,y)\ge2p-1\quad\text{a.e.}
> \]
> and
> \[
> p\ge0.629027936239236\ldots ,
> \]
> then the house conjecture holds.

---

# 5. A sharply isolated remaining half-density inequality

The interpolation \(W=s+(1-s)V\) reveals a particularly small non-flag target.

For an edge-\(1/2\) graphon \(V\), define
\[
S_m(V):=
\sum_{\substack{F\subseteq E(H)\\e(F)=m}}t(F,V).
\]
Then
\[
t(H,s+(1-s)V)
=
\sum_{m=0}^6s^{6-m}(1-s)^mS_m(V).
\tag{36}
\]

The target polynomial has the exact Bernstein expansion
\[
\begin{aligned}
B\!\left(\frac{1+s}{2}\right)
={}&s^6
+3s^5(1-s)
+\frac72s^4(1-s)^2\\
&+\frac{17}{8}s^3(1-s)^3
+\frac34s^2(1-s)^4
+\frac18s(1-s)^5.
\end{aligned}
\tag{37}
\]

The corresponding layer inequalities are elementary except at \(m=5\):
\[
S_0=1,\qquad S_1=3,
\]
\[
S_2\ge\frac{15}{4}>\frac72,
\qquad
S_3\ge\frac{19}{8}>\frac{17}{8},
\]
\[
S_4\ge\frac34,\qquad S_6\ge0.
\]

The only missing coefficient is
\[
\boxed{S_5(V)\stackrel{?}{\ge}\frac18.}
\tag{38}
\]

Writing the six edge-deleted graphs explicitly,
\[
\begin{aligned}
S_5(V)
={}&t(C_5,V)
+2t(C_4\text{ with a leaf},V)\\
&+2t(C_3\text{ with an attached }P_2,V)\\
&+t(C_3\text{ with two leaves},V).
\end{aligned}
\tag{39}
\]

For \(1/2\)-regular \(V\), leaf integration gives
\[
S_5(V)
=
\frac34t(C_3,V)+t(C_4,V)+t(C_5,V),
\]
so (38) follows from the spectral inequality (25). Thus the remaining issue in (38) is purely degree-irregular.

If (38) is proved, then comparison of (36) and (37) proves the house conjecture for every graphon satisfying
\[
W\ge2p-1
\]
throughout the complete interval \(p\ge1/2\). It is a five-edge quantum-graph inequality at the single fixed density \(1/2\), with no flags and no density parameter.

## Current boundary

The full conjecture remains open for arbitrary graphons in the lower-density range. What is now proved is:

\[
\begin{array}{c|c}
\text{graphon class}&\text{proved range}\\ \hline
\text{arbitrary graphons}
&p\ge0.7660575285\ldots\\[2mm]
p\text{-regular and }1-W\le2(1-p)
&p\ge1/2\\[2mm]
W\ge2p-1
&p\ge0.6290279362\ldots
\end{array}
\]

The most concrete next lemma is (38). Beyond the pointwise-floor class, the remaining analytic step is a clipping estimate showing that the contribution from the set
\[
\{(x,y):W(x,y)<2p-1\}
\]
is paid for by the degree-irregularity square \(\Phi_5\) and the triangle-tree surplus in (8).
