messages.text:
Consider a house graph, which has 5 vertices and 6 edges, that is constructed by gluing triangle and 4-cycle by an edge. 

Our conjecture is that this graph satisfies the following homomorphism density lower bound:
t(H, W) >= chi_H(1 / (1-p)) (1-p)^{v(H)} whenever p >= 1 - 1 / (chi(H) - 1)
where chi_H is the chromatic polynomial of H, v(H) is number of vertices in H, chi(H) is the chromatic number of H, and p is the edge density of W, t(K_2, W). 

This conjecture emerges from the turan graph optimality, if this conjecture is true, then the balanced complete k-partite graphons are minimisers of H-density under edge density constraints p = 1 - 1 / k. 

Work until you prove or disprove this conjecture.

## Status

I did **not** obtain a complete proof or a counterexample. The conjecture survives the exact reductions, local analysis, and structured-family tests below, but the remaining mixed path-kernel inequality is genuinely nontrivial. Thus the conclusions below are rigorous partial results, not a proof of the full statement.

Let \(H\) be the house graph with vertices \(u,v,a,b,c\) and edges
\[
uv,\ ua,\ va,\ ub,\ bc,\ cv.
\]
Equivalently, \(H\) is the generalized theta graph \(\Theta(1,2,3)\), with three internally disjoint \(u\)-\(v\) paths of lengths \(1,2,3\).

## 1. The conjectured bound explicitly

Because \(H\) is obtained by gluing \(K_3\) and \(C_4\) along \(K_2\),
\[
\chi_H(x)
=\frac{\chi_{K_3}(x)\chi_{C_4}(x)}{\chi_{K_2}(x)}
=x(x-1)(x-2)(x^2-3x+3).
\]
Thus \(\chi(H)=3\), so the relevant range is \(p\ge \tfrac12\). Writing \(q=1-p\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
(1-p)^5\chi_H\!\left(\frac1{1-p}\right)
&=p(2p-1)(p^3+q^3)\\
&=6p^4-9p^3+5p^2-p.
\end{aligned}
\]
The conjecture is therefore
\[
\boxed{\quad
t(H,W)\ge p(2p-1)\bigl(p^3+(1-p)^3\bigr),
\qquad p\ge\frac12.
\quad}
\tag{1}
\]

The normalization is exactly the one forced by balanced multipartite graphons: if \(T_k\) is the balanced complete \(k\)-partite graphon, then
\[
t(F,T_k)=\frac{\chi_F(k)}{k^{v(F)}},
\qquad
t(K_2,T_k)=1-\frac1k.
\]
This is the general motivation used in the pure-chordal note. fileciteturn0file1

The house is **not** covered by the pure-chordal theorem: its four cycle vertices induce a chordless \(C_4\), and its maximal cliques do not all have the same size. The tensor-product obstruction for graphs of even girth also does not apply, since the house has girth \(3\). fileciteturn0file2

## 2. Sharpness at every Turán density

For \(p=1-\frac1k\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
t(H,T_k)
&=\frac{k(k-1)(k-2)(k^2-3k+3)}{k^5}\\
&=p(2p-1)(p^3+q^3).
\end{aligned}
\]
Hence equality in (1) holds at every balanced complete \(k\)-partite graphon.

This confirms that the proposed right-hand side is the correct Turán interpolation polynomial.

## 3. The exact path-kernel formulation

Let \(T=T_W\) be the graphon operator, and write \(T^j(x,y)\) for the kernel of its \(j\)-th power. Rooting the three \(u\)-\(v\) paths of lengths \(1,2,3\) gives
\[
\boxed{\quad
t(H,W)
=
\int_{[0,1]^2}
W(x,y)\,T^2(x,y)\,T^3(x,y)\,dx\,dy.
\quad}
\tag{2}
\]

This is the central analytic difficulty. The analogous individual quantities are
\[
t(K_3,W)=\int W(x,y)T^2(x,y)\,dx\,dy
\]
and
\[
t(C_4,W)=\int W(x,y)T^3(x,y)\,dx\,dy.
\]
A generic edge-amalgamation inequality such as
\[
t(H,W)\stackrel{?}{\ge}
\frac{t(K_3,W)t(C_4,W)}{p}
\]
would immediately be useful, but such a positive-correlation assertion is not valid for arbitrary rooted extension kernels. The pure-chordal entropy argument works because all bags are identical cliques and have compatible separator marginals; that compatibility is absent for a triangle and a \(4\)-cycle.

## 4. An exact reduction to the sharp \(C_5\) inequality

The house is also obtained by adding a distance-two chord to \(C_5\). Put \(U=1-W\). If the added chord joins \(x_0\) and \(x_2\), define
\[
L(W):=
\int_{[0,1]^5}
U(x_0,x_2)
\prod_{i=0}^{4}W(x_i,x_{i+1})\,
dx_0\cdots dx_4,
\qquad x_5=x_0.
\]
Then
\[
t(H,W)=t(C_5,W)-L(W).
\tag{3}
\]
Equivalently,
\[
L(W)=\int U(x,y)T_W^2(x,y)T_W^3(x,y)\,dx\,dy.
\]

The audited odd-cycle result gives
\[
t(C_5,W)\ge g_5(p):=p^5-pq^4.
\]
fileciteturn0file0

A direct calculation shows
\[
g_5(p)-p(2p-1)(p^3+q^3)
=p^2q(2p-1).
\tag{4}
\]
Consequently, the house conjecture is equivalent to the following sharp chord-loss inequality:
\[
\boxed{\quad
L(W)
\le
\bigl[t(C_5,W)-(p^5-pq^4)\bigr]
+p^2q(2p-1).
\quad}
\tag{5}
\]

This reduction is useful because both terms on the right are nonnegative. It is also sharp: at every \(T_k\), the \(C_5\) surplus in brackets vanishes and
\[
L(T_k)=p^2q(2p-1).
\]
Thus a proof based on the \(C_5\) theorem must retain the deletion/chord-loss term quantitatively; simply bounding \(L\) by deleting some of its factors loses the required sharpness.

## 5. Strict first-order local minimality of every \(T_k\)

The balanced Turán graphon is not merely an equality example. It is a strict first-order local minimizer of the house density under the edge-density constraint.

For an edge \(e\in E(H)\), the chromatic polynomial of \(H/e\) depends on the position of \(e\). The relevant polynomials are

\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c}
\text{edge type}&\text{multiplicity}&\chi_{H/e}(x)\\ \hline
\text{shared triangle--square edge}&1&
x^4-4x^3+5x^2-2x\\
\text{other triangle edges}&2&
x^4-4x^3+6x^2-3x\\
\text{three remaining square edges}&3&
x^4-5x^3+8x^2-4x .
\end{array}
\]

Let \(F\) be a nonzero admissible first-order perturbation of \(T_k\) preserving edge density. Since \(T_k\) is \(0\)-\(1\)-valued, \(F\ge0\) on the within-part blocks and \(F\le0\) on the cross-part blocks. Put
\[
A_{\mathrm{in}}
=
\int_{\{\text{within the same part}\}}F.
\]
The edge constraint gives \(A_{\mathrm{out}}=-A_{\mathrm{in}}\), and \(A_{\mathrm{in}}>0\).

The first-variation kernel is constant on within-part blocks and on cross-part blocks. Its difference is
\[
K_{\mathrm{in}}-K_{\mathrm{out}}
=
\frac{
\displaystyle
\sum_{e\in E(H)}\chi_{H/e}(k)
-\frac{6}{k-1}\chi_H(k)
}{k^4}.
\]
Using the displayed contraction polynomials,
\[
\sum_{e\in E(H)}\chi_{H/e}(k)
-\frac{6}{k-1}\chi_H(k)
=
k(3k^2-13k+16).
\]
Therefore
\[
\delta t(H,T_k)[F]
=
\frac{3k^2-13k+16}{k^3}\,A_{\mathrm{in}}.
\]
Since
\[
3k^2-13k+16>0
\]
for every real \(k\) — its discriminant is \(169-192=-23\) — we obtain
\[
\boxed{\quad
\delta t(H,T_k)[F]>0
\quad}
\]
for every nonzero edge-preserving admissible direction.

Thus every \(T_k\) is a strict first-order local minimizer. This rules out all infinitesimal counterexamples around the proposed equality graphons, although it does not establish global minimality.

## 6. Exact verification on the natural near-bipartite family

Partition \([0,1]\) into two sets \(A,B\) of measure \(1/2\), and define
\[
W_r(x,y)=
\begin{cases}
1,&x\in A,\ y\in B\ \text{or conversely},\\
r,&x,y\in A\ \text{or}\ x,y\in B,
\end{cases}
\qquad 0\le r\le1.
\]
Its edge density is
\[
p=\frac{1+r}{2},
\qquad r=2p-1,
\]
and it is \(p\)-regular.

A direct enumeration of the \(2^5\) assignments of the house vertices to \(A,B\) gives
\[
t(H,W_r)
=
\frac{4r+6r^2+12r^3+8r^4+2r^6}{32}.
\]
In terms of \(p\) and \(q=1-p\), this is
\[
t(H,W_r)
=
p^6-p^3q^3+p^2q^4-pq^5.
\]
Subtracting the conjectured bound gives the exact factorization
\[
\boxed{\quad
t(H,W_r)-p(2p-1)(p^3+q^3)
=
p^2q^2(2p-1)^2
\ge0.
\quad}
\tag{6}
\]

Hence the conjecture holds on the equal-half near-bipartite family, with a quartically small margin near \(p=\frac12\). This is relevant because near-bipartite graphons are the most natural potential competitors close to the Mantel threshold.

The constant graphon \(W\equiv p\) is also safe:
\[
t(H,W)=p^6,
\]
and
\[
p^6-p(2p-1)(p^3+q^3)
=
p(1-p)^2\bigl(p^3+2p^2-3p+1\bigr)\ge0
\]
on \(p\in[\frac12,1]\).

## 7. What remains

The unresolved part is the global control of the interaction between the rooted length-\(2\) and length-\(3\) path kernels in (2), or equivalently the sharp chord-loss estimate (5). The available results establish:

\[
\begin{array}{c|c}
\text{class of graphons}&\text{status}\\ \hline
T_k&\text{equality}\\
\text{a neighborhood of }T_k\text{ at fixed edge density}
&\text{strict local inequality}\\
W\equiv p&\text{strict inequality except }p=1\\
\text{equal-half near-bipartite family}&\text{exact inequality (6)}\\
p=\frac12&\text{trivial, since the target is }0.
\end{array}
\]

The house is a generalized theta graph, but the existing generalized-theta literature concerns Sidorenko or KNRS-type statements and does not provide the fixed-edge chromatic-polynomial lower bound (1); in particular, the known regular or related theta results do not resolve the mixed nonregular optimization required here. citeturn129563search3turn129563search9

**Verdict:** no disproof emerged, and the exact local and structured-family calculations support the conjecture. However, a valid global proof has not been established. The sharp remaining statement is equation (5); proving it, likely through a retained-deletion sum-of-squares or flag-algebra certificate, would complete the conjecture.

I have stayed entirely within operator, entropy/gluing, spectral, and polynomial-certificate methods. I do **not** yet have the final global inequality, so the result below is not presented as a completed proof. There is, however, a substantially sharper reduction than before: the conjecture is now isolated to one explicit mixed path-kernel inequality, and in the regular case to a concrete Markov-kernel correlation inequality.

## 1. Two sharp lower bounds with the same missing term

Put
\[
q=1-p,\qquad r=2p-1,\qquad c=p^3+q^3.
\]
The desired inequality is
\[
t(H,W)\ge prc.
\tag{1}
\]

### 1.1 Chordal completion

Add either diagonal of the induced \(C_4\) in the house. The resulting graph \(F\) consists of three triangles arranged in a clique tree, with two edge separators. The pure-triangle-tree theorem therefore gives
\[
t(F,W)\ge p r^3.
\]
Since \(F\) is a supergraph of \(H\),
\[
t(H,W)\ge t(F,W)\ge pr^3.
\tag{2}
\]
This uses only the clique-tree gluing and Moon–Moser argument from the pure-chordal note. fileciteturn2file1

The difference between the conjectured target and (2) is exactly
\[
prc-pr^3
=pr(c-r^2)
=p^2qr,
\tag{3}
\]
because
\[
c-r^2=(p^3+q^3)-(2p-1)^2=pq.
\]

Thus the entire problem is the recovery of the single correction term
\[
p^2q(2p-1).
\]

### 1.2 The \(C_5\) reduction gives exactly the same correction

Write \(K_j^W(x,y)\) for the rooted \(j\)-edge path kernel, so that
\[
K_j^W(x,y)
=
\int W(x,z_1)W(z_1,z_2)\cdots W(z_{j-1},y)\,dz_1\cdots dz_{j-1}.
\]
The house is \(\Theta(1,2,3)\), hence
\[
t(H,W)=\int W(x,y)K_2^W(x,y)K_3^W(x,y)\,dx\,dy.
\tag{4}
\]

It is also a \(C_5\) with a distance-two chord. Therefore, with \(U=1-W\), define
\[
L(W):=
\int U(x,y)K_2^W(x,y)K_3^W(x,y)\,dx\,dy.
\tag{5}
\]
Then
\[
t(C_5,W)=t(H,W)+L(W).
\tag{6}
\]

The sharp \(C_5\) target is
\[
g_5(p)=p^5-pq^4.
\]
A direct calculation gives
\[
g_5(p)-prc=p^2qr.
\tag{7}
\]

The exact audited \(C_5\) certificate from the odd-cycle note is as follows. Let
\[
T=T_U,\qquad T1=q1+g,\qquad \langle g,1\rangle=0,
\]
and put
\[
x_4=t(P_4,U),\qquad c_5=t(C_5,U).
\]
Then
\[
t(C_5,W)-g_5(p)=\Phi_5(W)+\Gamma_5(W),
\tag{8}
\]
where
\[
\Gamma_5(W)=x_4-c_5
=
\int W(x_0,x_4)\prod_{i=0}^{3}U(x_i,x_{i+1})\,dx_0\cdots dx_4
\ge0
\tag{9}
\]
and
\[
\begin{aligned}
\Phi_5(W)
={}&4\|Tg\|_2^2+(8q-5)\langle g,Tg\rangle
 +(12q^2-15q+5)\|g\|_2^2\\
={}&4\left\|Tg+\frac{8q-5}{8}g\right\|_2^2
 +\left(8q^2-10q+\frac{55}{16}\right)\|g\|_2^2
\ge0.
\end{aligned}
\tag{10}
\]
This is the exact \(C_5\) certificate proved in the attached note. fileciteturn2file0

Combining (6)–(10) yields the exact identity
\[
\boxed{
t(H,W)-prc
=
\Phi_5(W)+\Gamma_5(W)+p^2qr-L(W).
}
\tag{11}
\]

Consequently, the house conjecture is **equivalent** to
\[
\boxed{
L(W)\le p^2q(2p-1)+\Phi_5(W)+\Gamma_5(W).
}
\tag{12}
\]

This is sharper than the earlier formulation because all terms are explicit:

- \(\Phi_5\) is an elementary Hilbert-space sum of squares;
- \(\Gamma_5\) is an explicit nonnegative deletion gap;
- only \(L(W)\) remains to be controlled.

At every balanced Turán graphon,
\[
\Phi_5=\Gamma_5=0,
\qquad
L=p^2qr,
\]
so (12) is tight term by term. In particular, the deletion gap cannot simply be discarded.

The tensor-product obstruction for graphs of even girth is irrelevant here: the house has girth \(3\), whereas that obstruction starts from an even shortest cycle. fileciteturn2file2

## 2. Exact reduction for regular graphons

There is a cleaner form of the problem when \(W\) is \(p\)-regular. Then \(U=1-W\) is \(q\)-regular. On the decomposition
\[
L^2([0,1])=\mathbb R1\oplus1^\perp
\]
we may write
\[
T_W=pJ-A,\qquad T_U=qJ+A,
\tag{13}
\]
where \(Jf=\langle f,1\rangle1\) and \(JA=AJ=0\).

It follows immediately that
\[
T_W^2-T_U^2=(p^2-q^2)J=rJ
\tag{14}
\]
and, since the third power is odd,
\[
T_W^3+T_U^3=(p^3+q^3)J=cJ.
\tag{15}
\]

Using (14)–(15) in (4) gives an exact identity. First,
\[
\begin{aligned}
t(H,W)
&=\int W K_2^W(c-K_3^U)\\
&=c\,t(K_3,W)
 -r\int W K_3^U
 -\int W K_2^U K_3^U.
\end{aligned}
\]
Regularity gives
\[
\int W K_3^U=q^3-t(C_4,U)
\tag{16}
\]
and
\[
\int W K_2^U K_3^U=t(C_5,U)-t(H,U).
\tag{17}
\]
Moreover,
\[
t(K_3,W)+t(K_3,U)=p^3+q^3=c.
\tag{18}
\]

Subtracting the target \(prc\), and using \(c-pr=q^2\), gives
\[
\boxed{
\begin{aligned}
t(H,W)-prc
={}&c\bigl(q^2-t(C_3,U)\bigr)
-r\bigl(q^3-t(C_4,U)\bigr)\\
&\quad-t(C_5,U)+t(H,U).
\end{aligned}}
\tag{19}
\]

This identity contains only cycle densities and the house density in the complement.

## 3. Markov-kernel form

Assume \(q>0\) and normalize
\[
U=qP.
\]
Then \(P\) is a symmetric Markov kernel:
\[
P\ge0,\qquad \int P(x,y)\,dy=1.
\]
Write
\[
\tau_j=t(C_j,P),\qquad \Theta=t(H,P).
\]
Since the house has six edges, (19) becomes
\[
\boxed{
\frac{t(H,W)-prc}{q^2}
=
c(1-q\tau_3)
-rq(1-q\tau_4)
-q^3\tau_5
+q^4\Theta.
}
\tag{20}
\]

Thus the regular case is reduced to the following completely explicit Markov-kernel inequality:
\[
\boxed{
c(1-q\tau_3)
-rq(1-q\tau_4)
-q^3\tau_5
+q^4\Theta\ge0.
}
\tag{21}
\]

No graph flags occur in (21).

## 4. A correlation inequality that would substantially close the regular case

The computational evidence points consistently to
\[
\boxed{
\Theta\ge \tau_3\tau_5
}
\tag{22}
\]
for every symmetric Markov kernel \(P\).

This is precisely
\[
t\!\left(C_3\mathbin{\cup_{P_2}}C_5,P\right)
\ge
t(C_3,P)t(C_5,P),
\tag{23}
\]
because \(t(P_2,P)=1\).

There is a useful two-stage formulation of (22). For \(a\in[0,1]\), let
\[
r_a(x)=P(a,x).
\]
Then
\[
\Theta
=
\int_a\int_{x,y}
r_a(x)r_a(y)P(x,y)P^3(x,y)\,dx\,dy\,da,
\tag{24}
\]
while
\[
P^3(a,a)
=
\int r_a(x)r_a(y)P(x,y)\,dx\,dy
\tag{25}
\]
and
\[
P^5(a,a)
=
\int r_a(x)r_a(y)P^3(x,y)\,dx\,dy.
\tag{26}
\]

Therefore (22) would follow from the two inequalities
\[
\int r(x)r(y)P(x,y)P^3(x,y)\,dx\,dy
\ge
\left(\int rrP\right)\left(\int rrP^3\right)
\tag{27}
\]
for every probability density \(r\), and
\[
\int P^3(a,a)P^5(a,a)\,da
\ge
\tau_3\tau_5.
\tag{28}
\]

I tested (27), (28), and (22) on large collections of finite symmetric Markov kernels, including convex combinations of symmetric permutation kernels, dense random kernels, nearly reducible kernels, and kernels with substantial negative spectrum. No violation was found. This is evidence only, not a proof.

A notable diagnostic is that the more general covariance
\[
\int rr\,P^aP^b
-
\left(\int rrP^a\right)\left(\int rrP^b\right)
\tag{29}
\]
appears nonnegative when \(a\) and \(b\) have the same parity, but can be negative when their parities differ. Thus (27) seems to be using a genuine parity-sensitive Markov correlation, rather than a generic positive-association assertion.

## 5. Spectral reduction after the correlation inequality

Suppose (22) is established. Let
\[
1,\lambda_1,\lambda_2,\ldots
\]
be the spectrum of \(T_P\), where \(1\) is the principal eigenvalue, and set
\[
s_j=\sum_{i\ge1}\lambda_i^j.
\]
Then
\[
\tau_j=1+s_j.
\]
Substituting \(\Theta\ge\tau_3\tau_5\) into (20), the required inequality follows from
\[
\boxed{
(p^3-q^3s_5)(p-qs_3)
\ge
rq(p-qs_4).
}
\tag{30}
\]

There is an elementary proof of (30) in the high-density range \(p\ge2/3\). Since
\[
\int U^2\le\int U=q,
\]
we have
\[
q(1+s_2)\le1.
\]
Put
\[
\delta=\frac pq-s_2\ge0
\]
and
\[
A_3=\sum_i\lambda_i^2(1-\lambda_i),\qquad
A_4=\sum_i\lambda_i^2(1-\lambda_i^2),\qquad
A_5=\sum_i\lambda_i^2(1-\lambda_i^3).
\]
Then
\[
p-qs_3=q(\delta+A_3),
\qquad
p-qs_4=q(\delta+A_4),
\tag{31}
\]
and
\[
p^3-q^3s_5=pr+q^3(\delta+A_5).
\tag{32}
\]
For every \(\lambda\in[-1,1]\),
\[
\lambda^2(1-\lambda^2)
=
(1+\lambda)\lambda^2(1-\lambda)
\le
2\lambda^2(1-\lambda),
\]
so
\[
\delta+A_4\le2(\delta+A_3).
\tag{33}
\]
After dividing (30) by \(q\), its left side minus its right side is at least
\[
\begin{aligned}
pr(\delta+A_3)-rq(\delta+A_4)
&\ge
pr(\delta+A_3)-2rq(\delta+A_3)\\
&=
r(p-2q)(\delta+A_3).
\end{aligned}
\]
This is nonnegative whenever \(p\ge2q\), equivalently \(p\ge2/3\).

Hence:

> **Conditional regular theorem.** If the Markov correlation inequality (22) holds, then the house conjecture holds for every \(p\)-regular graphon in the range \(p\ge2/3\).

For \(1/2\le p\le2/3\), the crude estimate \(A_4\le2A_3\) is insufficient, and the full Markov constraints must be used.

## 6. Why a spectral Bernstein certificate alone is not enough

It is tempting to treat the \(\lambda_i\) merely as numbers satisfying
\[
-1\le\lambda_i\le1,
\qquad
q(1+s_2)\le1,
\]
and prove (30) by Bernstein subdivision. That relaxation is too large: artificial spectral sequences satisfying these conditions can violate (30). Such sequences need not be spectra of an entrywise nonnegative Markov kernel.

Therefore a successful computational certificate must retain at least one of:

1. the correlation term \(\Theta-\tau_3\tau_5\);
2. entrywise nonnegativity of the Markov kernel;
3. the coupling between eigenvalues and eigenfunctions;
4. in the general irregular case, the deletion term \(\Gamma_5\) in (11).

A Bernstein certificate over only \((q,s_2,s_3,s_4,s_5)\) is unlikely to be valid.

Let
\[

\]
be the rooted two-edge path kernel, and define
\[
A(x,y):=W(x,y)C(x,y),\qquad
D(x,y):=(1-W(x,y))C(x,y).
\]
Thus
\[
A+D=C.
\]

Consider a \(5\)-cycle in the form
\[
y-a-x-b-z-y.
\]
The two distance-two chords incident to \(x\) are \(xy\) and \(xz\). Define
\[
\begin{aligned}
F&:=\int W(y,z)A(x,y)A(x,z)\,dx\,dy\,dz,\\
R&:=\int W(y,z)A(x,y)D(x,z)\,dx\,dy\,dz,\\
G&:=\int W(y,z)D(x,y)D(x,z)\,dx\,dy\,dz.
\end{aligned}
\tag{2}
\]
By symmetry, the density with \(D(x,y)A(x,z)\) is also \(R\).

Expanding \(C=A+D\) gives
\[
t(C_5,W)=F+2R+G.
\tag{3}
\]
On the other hand, imposing the chord \(xy\) produces the house, so
\[
t(H,W)=F+R.
\tag{4}
\]
Therefore
\[
\boxed{\;
2t(H,W)=F+t(C_5,W)-G.
\;}
\tag{5}
\]

The interpretation is useful:

- \(F\) is the density where both distance-two chords are present;
- \(G\) is the density where both are absent;
- the two mixed cases are the two symmetric realizations of the house.

## 6. A further result for regular graphons

The same decomposition gives a stronger threshold in the regular case.

Suppose \(W\) is \(p\)-regular. Then \(U\) is \(q\)-regular, so \(g=0\), \(\Phi_5=0\), and
\[
\delta=n.
\tag{27}
\]
Moreover,
\[
C_W(x,y)=r+C_U(x,y).
\]
Set
\[
K(x,y):=U(x,y)C_U(x,y).
\]
Then
\[
D=rU+K.
\tag{28}
\]

For nonnegative kernels \(K_1,K_2\), put
\[
\mathcal Q(K_1,K_2)
=
\int W(y,z)K_1(x,y)K_2(x,z)\,dx\,dy\,dz.
\]
Since \(U\) is \(q\)-regular,
\[
C_U(x,y)\le q,
\]
and therefore
\[
K\le qU,\qquad K\le C_U.
\]
It follows that
\[
\begin{aligned}
G
&=\mathcal Q(rU+K,rU+K)\\
&=r^2n+2r\mathcal Q(U,K)+\mathcal Q(K,K)\\
&\le r^2n+2rq\,n+\Gamma_5\\
&=\Gamma_5+r n.
\end{aligned}
\tag{29}
\]
Here we used
\[
r^2+2rq=r(r+2q)=r.
\]

Substituting this into (23),
\[
\begin{aligned}
2\bigl(t(H,W)-B(p)\bigr)
&\ge
(3r^2-r)n
+\frac{3r}{p}n^2
+\frac{n^3}{p^2}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{30}
\]
Hence this is nonnegative whenever \(3r\ge1\), namely \(p\ge2/3\).

> **Regular-graphon theorem.** If \(W\) is \(p\)-regular and
> \[
> p\ge\frac23,
> \]
> then the house conjecture holds.

```latex
p^5-pq^4
=
p(p^4-q^4)
\le0,
\]
and the assertion follows from \(t(C_5,W)\ge0\).  Hence it is enough to
consider
\[
0\le q\le\frac12.
\]

For \(j\ge1\), let
\[
x_j:=t(P_j,U),
\]
where \(P_j\) denotes the path with \(j\) edges, and put
\[
c_5:=t(C_5,U).
\]

Expanding
\[
t(C_5,W)=t(C_5,1-U)
\]
by inclusion--exclusion over the five edges of \(C_5\) gives
\[
t(C_5,1-U)
=
1-5q+5x_2+5q^2
-5x_3-5qx_2+5x_4-c_5.
\]
Since \(0\le U\le1\), deleting one edge from the integrand defining
\(c_5\) gives
\[
c_5\le x_4.
\]
Therefore
\[
t(C_5,1-U)
\ge
1-5q+5q^2
+5(1-q)x_2
-5x_3
+4x_4.
\]
On the other hand,
\[
(1-q)^5-(1-q)q^4
=
1-5q+10q^2-10q^3+4q^4.
\]
Thus it is enough to prove
\begin{equation}\label{eq:c5certificate}
4x_4-5x_3+5(1-q)x_2
-
\bigl(4q^4-10q^3+5q^2\bigr)
\ge0.
\end{equation}

Let \(T=T_U\) be the self-adjoint graphon operator
\[
Tf(x)
=
\int_0^1U(x,y)f(y)\,\dd y.
\]
Write
\[
T\one=q\one+g,
\qquad
\ip{g}{\one}=0.
\]
We compute the first three path moments.

First,
\[
x_2
=
\|T\one\|_2^2
=
q^2+\|g\|_2^2.
\]
Next,
\[
T^2\one
=
T(q\one+g)
=
q^2\one+qg+Tg,
\]
and hence
\[
\begin{aligned}
x_3
&=
\ip{T\one}{T^2\one}\\
&=
\ip{q\one+g}{q^2\one+qg+Tg}\\
&=
q^3+2q\|g\|_2^2+\ip{g}{Tg},
\end{aligned}
\]
where we used
\[
\ip{\one}{Tg}
=
\ip{T\one}{g}
=
\|g\|_2^2.
\]
Finally,
\[
x_4
=
\|T^2\one\|_2^2,
\]
so
\[
x_4
=
q^4
+3q^2\|g\|_2^2
+2q\ip{g}{Tg}
+\|Tg\|_2^2.
\]

Substitution into the left-hand side of
\eqref{eq:c5certificate} gives
\[
4\|Tg\|_2^2
+
(8q-5)\ip{g}{Tg}
+
(12q^2-15q+5)\|g\|_2^2.
\]
Completing the square,
\[
\begin{aligned}
&4\|Tg\|_2^2
+
(8q-5)\ip{g}{Tg}
+
(12q^2-15q+5)\|g\|_2^2\\
&\qquad=
4\left\|
Tg+\frac{8q-5}{8}g
\right\|_2^2
+
\left(
8q^2-10q+\frac{55}{16}
\right)
\|g\|_2^2.
\end{aligned}
\]
The remaining scalar coefficient is strictly positive:
\[
8q^2-10q+\frac{55}{16}
=
8\left(q-\frac58\right)^2+\frac5{16}>0.
\]
Thus \eqref{eq:c5certificate} holds, completing the proof.
\end{proof}

\section{A three-triangle gluing inequality}

We now prove the special clique-tree inequality needed in the main
argument directly in graphon space.

For a graphon \(W\), define its two-step kernel
\[
C_W(x,y)
:=
\int_0^1W(x,s)W(s,y)\,\dd s.
\]

Let \(F\) be the graph on five vertices \(x,y,z,a,b\) whose three maximal
cliques are
\[
\{x,y,z\},\qquad
\{x,y,a\},\qquad
\{x,z,b\}.
\]
Thus \(F\) consists of three triangles, with the first triangle sharing
the edge \(xy\) with the second and the edge \(xz\) with the third.

\begin{lemma}[Three-triangle gluing]\label{lem:triangle-tree}
Let
\[
p=t(K_2,W),
\qquad
\tau=t(K_3,W).
\]
If \(p>0\), then
\[
\boxed{
t(F,W)\ge\frac{\tau^3}{p^2}.
}
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
If \(\tau=0\), the claim is immediate.  Assume henceforth that
\(\tau>0\).

Write simply
\[
C(x,y):=C_W(x,y).
\]
Integrating first over the two vertices \(a,b\) gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:F-density}
t(F,W)
=
\int_{[0,1]^3}
W(x,y)W(x,z)W(y,z)
C(x,y)C(x,z)
\,\dd x\,\dd y\,\dd z.
\end{equation}

Consider the probability density
\[
\rho(x,y,z)
:=
\frac{
W(x,y)W(x,z)W(y,z)
}{\tau}
\]
on \([0,1]^3\).
Its \((x,y)\)-marginal is the probability density
\[
\nu(x,y)
=
\frac{W(x,y)C(x,y)}{\tau}.
\]
The \((x,z)\)-marginal is the same, after relabelling variables.

Also consider the probability density
\[
\mu(x,y)
=
\frac{W(x,y)}{p}
\]
on \([0,1]^2\).
We have \(\nu\ll\mu\), with Radon--Nikodym derivative
\[
\frac{\dd\nu}{\dd\mu}(x,y)
=
\frac{p\,C(x,y)}{\tau}.
\]
Nonnegativity of relative entropy gives
\[
0
\le
D(\nu\Vert\mu)
=
\int_{[0,1]^2}
\nu(x,y)
\log\left(
\frac{pC(x,y)}{\tau}
\right)
\,\dd x\,\dd y.
\]
Therefore
\begin{equation}\label{eq:geom-codegree}
\int\nu(x,y)\log C(x,y)\,\dd x\,\dd y
\ge
\log\frac{\tau}{p}.
\end{equation}

By \eqref{eq:F-density},
\[
\frac{t(F,W)}{\tau}
=
\mathbb E_\rho
\bigl[
C(x,y)C(x,z)
\bigr].
\]
Jensen's inequality for the concave function \(\log\) gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
\log\frac{t(F,W)}{\tau}
&\ge
\mathbb E_\rho
\bigl[
\log C(x,y)+\log C(x,z)
\bigr]\\
&=
2\int\nu(x,y)\log C(x,y)\,\dd x\,\dd y\\
&\ge
2\log\frac{\tau}{p},
\end{aligned}
\]
where the last inequality is \eqref{eq:geom-codegree}.
Exponentiating,
\[
\frac{t(F,W)}{\tau}
\ge
\left(\frac{\tau}{p}\right)^2,
\]
hence
\[
t(F,W)\ge\frac{\tau^3}{p^2}.
\]

All logarithmic expressions above may be interpreted in the usual
extended sense.  Alternatively, one may replace \(C\) by
\(C+\varepsilon\), apply the same argument, and let
\(\varepsilon\downarrow0\).
\end{proof}

\section{The exact two-chord decomposition}

We now turn to the house graph.

Let
\[
U:=1-W.
\]
Again write
\[
C(x,y)
=
C_W(x,y)
=
\int_0^1W(x,s)W(s,y)\,\dd s.
\]
Define
\[
A(x,y):=W(x,y)C(x,y),
\qquad
D(x,y):=U(x,y)C(x,y).
\]
Since \(W+U=1\),
\begin{equation}\label{eq:AplusD}
A(x,y)+D(x,y)=C(x,y).
\end{equation}

Consider the \(5\)-cycle
\[
x-a-y-z-b-x.
\]
After integrating over \(a\) and \(b\), its density is
\[
t(C_5,W)
=
\int_{[0,1]^3}
W(y,z)C(x,y)C(x,z)
\,\dd x\,\dd y\,\dd z.
\]
The two distance-two chords incident with \(x\) are \(xy\) and \(xz\).

Define
\[
\begin{aligned}
F
&:=
\int
W(y,z)A(x,y)A(x,z)
\,\dd x\,\dd y\,\dd z,\\
R
&:=
\int
W(y,z)A(x,y)D(x,z)
\,\dd x\,\dd y\,\dd z,\\
G
&:=
\int
W(y,z)D(x,y)D(x,z)
\,\dd x\,\dd y\,\dd z.
\end{aligned}
\]
The integral with \(D(x,y)A(x,z)\) instead of
\(A(x,y)D(x,z)\) also equals \(R\), by interchanging \(y\) and \(z\).

Expanding \eqref{eq:AplusD} therefore gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:c5split}
t(C_5,W)=F+2R+G.
\end{equation}

On the other hand, adding the chord \(xy\) to the \(5\)-cycle gives
exactly the house graph: \(xay\) is the triangle and
\(xy z b x\) is the \(4\)-cycle.
Consequently
\[
\begin{aligned}
t(H,W)
&=
\int
W(y,z)A(x,y)C(x,z)
\,\dd x\,\dd y\,\dd z\\
&=
F+R.
\end{aligned}
\]
Combining this with \eqref{eq:c5split}, we obtain the exact identity
\begin{equation}\label{eq:key-decomposition}
\boxed{
2t(H,W)
=
F+t(C_5,W)-G.
}
\end{equation}

This identity is the main structural point of the proof.

\section{Triangle surplus and the bad two-chord term}

Let
\[
\tau:=t(K_3,W)
\]
and define the Goodman surplus
\[
\delta
:=
\tau-p(2p-1)
=
\tau-pr.
\]
By Lemma~\ref{lem:goodman},
\begin{equation}\label{eq:delta-nonneg}
\delta\ge0.
\end{equation}

We shall show that the negative term \(G\) in
\eqref{eq:key-decomposition} is bounded by this same surplus.

Let
\[
d_U(x):=\int_0^1U(x,y)\,\dd y
\]
and
\[
x_2:=t(P_2,U)
=
\int_0^1d_U(x)^2\,\dd x.
\]
Since
\[
\int_0^1d_U(x)\,\dd x=q,
\]
put
\[
v
:=
x_2-q^2
=
\int_0^1(d_U(x)-q)^2\,\dd x
\ge0.
\]
Also define
\begin{equation}\label{eq:n-def}
n
:=
\int_{[0,1]^3}
W(y,z)U(x,y)U(x,z)
\,\dd x\,\dd y\,\dd z.
\end{equation}
Clearly
\[
n\ge0.
\]

Let
\[
\kappa_3:=t(K_3,U).
\]
Splitting the missing edge \(yz\) according to
\(1=W(y,z)+U(y,z)\), we have
\[
x_2=n+\kappa_3,
\]
and hence
\begin{equation}\label{eq:n-x2}
n=x_2-\kappa_3.
\end{equation}

Expanding the triangle density of \(W=1-U\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
\tau
&=
t(K_3,1-U)\\
&=
1-3q+3x_2-\kappa_3.
\end{aligned}
\]
Since
\[
pr
=
(1-q)(1-2q)
=
1-3q+2q^2,
\]
we obtain
\[
\begin{aligned}
\delta
&=
\tau-pr\\
&=
3x_2-\kappa_3-2q^2\\
&=
2(x_2-q^2)+(x_2-\kappa_3).
\end{aligned}
\]
Using the definitions of \(v\) and \(n\),
\begin{equation}\label{eq:delta-decomp}
\boxed{
\delta=2v+n.
}
\end{equation}
In particular,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:n-le-delta}
0\le n\le\delta.
\end{equation}

Now \(0\le C(x,y)\le1\), and therefore
\[
0\le D(x,y)
=
U(x,y)C(x,y)
\le U(x,y).
\]
It follows directly from the definition of \(G\) that
\[
\begin{aligned}
G
&=
\int
W(y,z)
D(x,y)D(x,z)
\,\dd x\,\dd y\,\dd z\\
&\le
\int
W(y,z)
U(x,y)U(x,z)
\,\dd x\,\dd y\,\dd z\\
&=
n.
\end{aligned}
\]
Together with \eqref{eq:n-le-delta}, this gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:G-delta}
\boxed{
G\le n\le\delta.
}
\end{equation}

\section{Completion of the proof}

We can now prove Theorem~\ref{thm:main}.

\begin{proof}[Proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:main}]
Assume
\[
p\ge\frac{1+1/\sqrt3}{2}.
\]
In particular \(p>1/2\), so
\[
r:=2p-1>0.
\]
Let
\[
q:=1-p,
\qquad
c:=p^3+q^3,
\qquad
B(p):=prc.
\]
Thus \(B(p)\) is precisely the claimed chromatic-polynomial lower bound.

Let
\[
\tau=t(K_3,W)=pr+\delta,
\qquad
\delta\ge0.
\]

The graph counted by \(F\) is exactly the graph of
Lemma~\ref{lem:triangle-tree}, so
\[
F\ge\frac{\tau^3}{p^2}.
\]
Therefore
\[
\begin{aligned}
F-pr^3
&\ge
\frac{(pr+\delta)^3}{p^2}-pr^3\\
&=
3r^2\delta
+
\frac{3r}{p}\delta^2
+
\frac1{p^2}\delta^3.
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus
\begin{equation}\label{eq:F-surplus}
F-pr^3
\ge
3r^2\delta
+
\frac{3r}{p}\delta^2
+
\frac1{p^2}\delta^3.
\end{equation}

By Lemma~\ref{lem:c5},
\begin{equation}\label{eq:C5-surplus}
t(C_5,W)
\ge
p^5-pq^4.
\end{equation}
Since \(p+q=1\) and \(r=p-q\),
\[
p^5-pq^4
=
p(p^4-q^4)
=
pr(p^2+q^2).
\]
Moreover,
\[
\begin{aligned}
r^2+p^2+q^2
&=
(p-q)^2+p^2+q^2\\
&=
2(p^2-pq+q^2)\\
&=
2(p^3+q^3),
\end{aligned}
\]
where in the last equality we used
\[
p^3+q^3=(p+q)^3-3pq(p+q)=1-3pq
=p^2-pq+q^2.
\]
Consequently,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:target-split}
pr^3+\bigl(p^5-pq^4\bigr)
=
pr\bigl(r^2+p^2+q^2\bigr)
=
2pr(p^3+q^3)
=
2B(p).
\end{equation}

Subtracting \eqref{eq:target-split} from the exact decomposition
\eqref{eq:key-decomposition}, we obtain the exact defect identity
\begin{equation}\label{eq:defect-exact}
\boxed{
\begin{aligned}
2\bigl(t(H,W)-B(p)\bigr)
={}&
\bigl(F-pr^3\bigr)\\
&+
\bigl(t(C_5,W)-(p^5-pq^4)\bigr)
-G.
\end{aligned}
}
\end{equation}

The middle term is nonnegative by
\eqref{eq:C5-surplus}.  Combining
\eqref{eq:F-surplus} and \eqref{eq:G-delta} with
\eqref{eq:defect-exact} gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
2\bigl(t(H,W)-B(p)\bigr)
&\ge
3r^2\delta
+
\frac{3r}{p}\delta^2
+
\frac1{p^2}\delta^3
-G\\
&\ge
3r^2\delta
+
\frac{3r}{p}\delta^2
+
\frac1{p^2}\delta^3
-\delta\\
&=
(3r^2-1)\delta
+
\frac{3r}{p}\delta^2
+
\frac1{p^2}\delta^3.
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus we have proved the quantitative estimate
\begin{equation}\label{eq:quantitative-final}
\boxed{
2\bigl(t(H,W)-B(p)\bigr)
\ge
(3r^2-1)\delta
+
\frac{3r}{p}\delta^2
+
\frac1{p^2}\delta^3.
}
\end{equation}

Finally, the hypothesis
\[
p\ge\frac{1+1/\sqrt3}{2}
\]
is equivalent, because \(r=2p-1\ge0\), to
\[
r\ge\frac1{\sqrt3},
\]
and hence
\[
3r^2-1\ge0.
\]
Every term on the right-hand side of
\eqref{eq:quantitative-final} is therefore nonnegative, since
\[
p>0,\qquad r\ge0,\qquad \delta\ge0.
\]
It follows that
\[
t(H,W)\ge B(p)
=
p(2p-1)(p^3+q^3).
\]
Since \(q=1-p\),
\[
t(H,W)
\ge
p(2p-1)
\bigl(p^3+(1-p)^3\bigr).
\]
As shown at the beginning,
\[
p(2p-1)
\bigl(p^3+(1-p)^3\bigr)
=
(1-p)^5
\chi_H\!\left(\frac1{1-p}\right).
\]
This proves the theorem.
\end{proof}

\section{A useful quantitative form}

The proof actually establishes a little more than the theorem.

\begin{proposition}\label{prop:quantitative}
Let \(W\) be any graphon with \(p>1/2\).  Put
\[
r=2p-1
\]
and
\[
\delta
=
t(K_3,W)-p(2p-1)\ge0.
\]
Then
\[
\boxed{
\begin{aligned}
2\Bigl(
t(H,W)
-
p(2p-1)
\bigl(p^3+(1-p)^3\bigr)
\Bigr)
\ge{}&
(3(2p-1)^2-1)\delta\\
&+
\frac{3(2p-1)}{p}\delta^2
+
\frac1{p^2}\delta^3.
\end{aligned}
}
\]
In particular, the desired house inequality follows whenever
\[
3(2p-1)^2\ge1.
\]
\end{proposition}

\begin{remark}
The argument is sharp at every balanced complete \(k\)-partite graphon
whose edge density lies in the proved range.  At such a graphon,
\[
p=1-\frac1k,
\]
the Goodman triangle surplus satisfies
\[
\delta=0,
\]
the \(C_5\) inequality is an equality, and the term \(G\) is zero.
Thus no positive error is introduced at the Tur\'an equality examples.
For the present density range, this includes every \(k\ge5\).
\end{remark}

\end{document}
```

The key quantitative conclusion to preserve in any later formalization is
\[
2\bigl(t(H,W)-B(p)\bigr)
\ge
\bigl(3(2p-1)^2-1\bigr)\delta
+\frac{3(2p-1)}p\delta^2
+\frac1{p^2}\delta^3,
\qquad
\delta=t(K_3,W)-p(2p-1).
\]
So after the exact two-chord identity, the threshold \((1+1/\sqrt3)/2\) is not an artifact of further estimates: it comes precisely from paying the bad term \(G\le\delta\) using the linear part \(3(2p-1)^2\delta\) of the three-triangle gluing surplus.

In this article, we prove that some condition implies that the graph satisfies some Goodman-style lower bound on the homomorphism density. 
On the paper by Grzesik, Lee, Lidický, and Volec, they have some robustness result, not just exact condition, that when it is allowed to add edges. Would you please check their statement, and see if we can extend this proof by allowing some edge robustness?

For some context, this argument often fails on general chordal graph. For instance, adding 20 edges each vertex to triangle makes the graph still chordal, but creates counterexample for the conjectured lower bound. So this theory is not robust on the pendant edge. If we can give some bound on the number... we it would be much more strong result.

If I'm understanding correctly, you didn't prove tighter result or something similar, but interpreted the existing result in terms of robustness, right? In other words, the graphs that can be proven to satisfy this Goodman style lower bound by entropic theorem is still same. Right?

messages.text:
In this article, we prove that some condition implies that the graph satisfies some Goodman-style lower bound on the homomorphism density. 
On the paper by Grzesik, Lee, Lidický, and Volec, they have some robustness result, not just exact condition, that when it is allowed to add edges. Would you please check their statement, and see if we can extend this proof by allowing some edge robustness?

For some context, this argument often fails on general chordal graph. For instance, adding 20 edges each vertex to triangle makes the graph still chordal, but creates counterexample for the conjectured lower bound. So this theory is not robust on the pendant edge. If we can give some bound on the number... we it would be much more strong result.

## Main conclusion

Yes. The robustness mechanism of Grzesik–Lee–Lidický–Volec transfers to the chromatic-polynomial lower bound, and in the notation of your article the natural pendant-edge budget is

\[
\boxed{\rho_2(H):=b_3(H)-b_2(H).}
\]

More precisely, suppose \(H\) satisfies the monotone exponent condition

\[
b_1(H)\le b_2(H)\le\cdots\le b_r(H).
\]

Then one may attach arbitrary pendant trees, at arbitrary vertices and with arbitrary branching, provided that their **total number of edges** is at most \(b_3-b_2\). The resulting graph still satisfies the same Goodman-style lower bound.

This is not merely analogous to the Grzesik–Lee–Lidický–Volec theorem: on pure triangle-trees it recovers exactly their numerical robustness parameter.

---

## 1. What the Grzesik–Lee–Lidický–Volec result says

For a triangle-tree \(H\), they define

\[
\varphi(H):=e(H)-v(H)+1,
\qquad
\kappa(H):=2e(H)-3v(H)+3.
\]

Here \(\varphi(H)\) is the number of triangle bags, while \(\kappa(H)\) is the number of edges of a triangle decomposition whose separator is a \(K_2\).

Their Theorem 1.2 states that if \(T\) is any tree and

\[
e(T)\le \kappa(H),
\]

then the graph \(T*_u^vH\), obtained by identifying an arbitrary vertex \(u\in V(T)\) with an arbitrary vertex \(v\in V(H)\), remains common.

The part directly relevant to your problem is their one-colour Lemma 3.6:

\[
t(T*_u^vH,W)
\ge
\frac{t(K_3,W)^{\varphi(H)}}
     {t(K_2,W)^{\kappa(H)-e(T)}}.
\tag{1}
\]

Their subsequent commonality argument applies (1) to \(W\) and \(1-W\). Thus, although their headline theorem concerns commonality, the actual entropy lemma is already an edge-density-sensitive, one-colour inequality. fileciteturn0file0

The mechanism is particularly transparent. Every triangle bag is sampled from the uniform labelled-triangle distribution. Its two-coordinate marginal is an edge distribution weighted by the number of triangles containing the edge. Each \(K_2\)-separator contributes a negative copy of the entropy of this projected edge law, while each newly added tree edge contributes a positive copy. Consequently, one pendant-tree edge cancels one \(K_2\)-separator term.

---

## 2. Pendant-forest robustness for the theorem in your article

Call \(\widehat H\) a pendant-forest extension of \(H\) with \(\ell\) edges if it can be obtained through \(\ell\) successive operations, each adding a new vertex adjacent to exactly one previously present vertex.

Equivalently, one may attach an arbitrary finite collection of rooted trees to arbitrary vertices of \(H\), with total number of tree edges \(\ell\).

### Theorem

Let \(H\) be a connected chordal graph with clique number \(r\ge 3\), and suppose

\[
b_1(H)\le b_2(H)\le\cdots\le b_r(H).
\]

Let \(\widehat H\) be any pendant-forest extension of \(H\) with \(\ell\) edges. If

\[
\boxed{\ell\le b_3(H)-b_2(H),}
\tag{2}
\]

then every graphon \(W\) with edge density

\[
p=t(K_2,W)\ge 1-\frac1{r-1}
\]

satisfies

\[
\boxed{
t(\widehat H,W)
\ge
\Phi_{\widehat H}(p)
=
p^\ell\Phi_H(p).
}
\tag{3}
\]

### Proof

Consider first one leaf addition. Let \(x\) be the new vertex and let \(y\) be its unique neighbour.

The edge \(\{x,y\}\) is a new maximal clique of size two. Given a clique tree of \(H\), choose any maximal clique containing \(y\), and attach the new bag \(\{x,y\}\) to that clique. The resulting separator is the one-vertex clique \(\{y\}\).

Therefore one leaf addition has the following effect:

- it adds one maximal clique of size \(2\);
- it adds one clique-tree separator of size \(1\).

Recalling

\[
b_j=
\#\{i:r_i\ge j\}
-
\#\{e:s_e\ge j\},
\]

the change is

\[
b_1\longmapsto b_1,
\qquad
b_2\longmapsto b_2+1,
\qquad
b_j\longmapsto b_j\quad(j\ge 3).
\]

After \(\ell\) such additions,

\[
b_j(\widehat H)=
\begin{cases}
b_1(H),&j=1,\\[2mm]
b_2(H)+\ell,&j=2,\\[2mm]
b_j(H),&3\le j\le r.
\end{cases}
\tag{4}
\]

Condition (2) gives

\[
b_1(H)
\le b_2(H)+\ell
\le b_3(H)
\le\cdots\le b_r(H).
\]

Thus \(\widehat H\) still satisfies the monotone exponent condition, so the main theorem of your article applies.

It remains to identify its target polynomial. Each added leaf multiplies the chromatic polynomial by \(x-1\). Hence

\[
\chi_{\widehat H}(x)
=
\chi_H(x)(x-1)^\ell,
\qquad
v(\widehat H)=v(H)+\ell.
\]

Writing \(q=1-p\),

\[
\begin{aligned}
\Phi_{\widehat H}(p)
&=
q^{v(H)+\ell}
\chi_H(1/q)(1/q-1)^\ell\\
&=
\Phi_H(p)\bigl(q(1/q-1)\bigr)^\ell\\
&=
p^\ell\Phi_H(p).
\end{aligned}
\]

This proves (3).

---

## 3. Structural form of the budget

Let

\[
m_2:=\#\{\text{maximal cliques of }H\text{ having size }2\},
\]

and let

\[
a_2:=\#\{\text{clique-tree edges whose separator has size }2\}.
\]

Your identity

\[
b_{j+1}-b_j=a_j-m_j
\]

gives, at \(j=2\),

\[
\boxed{
b_3-b_2=a_2-m_2.
}
\tag{5}
\]

Thus the robustness budget has an intrinsic structural interpretation:

\[
\boxed{
\text{permitted pendant-tree edges}
\le
\#\{K_2\text{-separators}\}
-
\#\{\text{maximal }K_2\text{ cliques}\}.
}
\]

The subtraction by \(m_2\) is natural. Every maximal \(K_2\) already behaves, in the entropy calculation, like one pendant edge and therefore already consumes one available \(K_2\)-separator term.

For an \(r\)-pure chordal graph, \(m_2=0\). Consequently:

\[
\boxed{\ell\le a_2}
\tag{6}
\]

is sufficient.

The bound concerns the total number of attached edges. Their locations do not matter: they may all be attached at one vertex, distributed among many vertices, or arranged into arbitrarily branching trees.

---

## 4. Exact recovery of the triangle-tree theorem

Let \(H\) be a pure triangle-tree. Put

\[
m:=\varphi(H),
\qquad
\kappa:=\kappa(H).
\]

There are \(m\) maximal triangle bags and exactly \(\kappa\) edge separators. Therefore

\[
b_2(H)=m-\kappa,
\qquad
b_3(H)=m,
\]

and hence

\[
b_3(H)-b_2(H)=\kappa.
\]

Thus condition (2) becomes precisely

\[
e(T)\le\kappa(H),
\]

the same numerical threshold as in Grzesik–Lee–Lidický–Volec.

Moreover,

\[
\Phi_H(p)=p^{m-\kappa}(2p-1)^m.
\]

After attaching a tree with \(\ell=e(T)\) edges,

\[
\Phi_{T*H}(p)
=
p^{m-\kappa+\ell}(2p-1)^m.
\tag{7}
\]

Their density inequality (1), together with the Goodman–Moon–Moser triangle inequality

\[
t(K_3,W)\ge p(2p-1),
\qquad p\ge\frac12,
\]

gives

\[
\begin{aligned}
t(T*H,W)
&\ge
\frac{t(K_3,W)^m}{p^{\kappa-\ell}}\\
&\ge
\frac{\bigl(p(2p-1)\bigr)^m}{p^{\kappa-\ell}}\\
&=
p^{m-\kappa+\ell}(2p-1)^m\\
&=
\Phi_{T*H}(p).
\end{aligned}
\]

So, for pure triangle-trees, their entropy lemma proves exactly the chromatic-polynomial lower bound after the permitted pendant-tree attachment.

---

## 5. A stronger density inequality for pure \(r\)-chordal cores

The same projected-edge construction works with \(K_r\) in place of \(K_3\).

Let \(H\) be \(r\)-pure chordal. Write:

- \(m\) for the number of maximal \(K_r\)-bags;
- \(a_s\) for the number of clique-tree separators of size exactly \(s\);
- \(t_s=t(K_s,W)\).

Let \(\widehat H\) be obtained by attaching a pendant forest with \(\ell\le a_2\) edges. Then

\[
\boxed{
t(\widehat H,W)
\ge
\frac{t_r^m}
{t_2^{\,a_2-\ell}\displaystyle\prod_{s=3}^{r-1}t_s^{a_s}}.
}
\tag{8}
\]

When a denominator vanishes, this should be read in its cross-multiplied form.

To see this, assign the uniform \(K_r\)-homomorphism law to each core bag and its two-coordinate marginal to every new edge bag. If \(\mathcal H_s\) denotes the entropy of an \(s\)-coordinate marginal, junction-tree entropy gives

\[
\log\hom(\widehat H,G)
\ge
m\log h_r
-
(a_2-\ell)\mathcal H_2
-
\sum_{s=3}^{r-1}a_s\mathcal H_s
-
(a_1+\ell)\mathcal H_1.
\tag{9}
\]

The assumption \(\ell\le a_2\) makes all the displayed entropy coefficients nonpositive. Consequently,

\[
\mathcal H_s\le\log h_s,
\qquad
\mathcal H_1\le\log n
\]

can be applied in the correct direction. Normalisation yields (8).

Finally, the Moon–Moser clique-ratio inequalities give

\[
\frac{t_r}{t_s}\ge\frac{A_r(p)}{A_s(p)},
\qquad
t_r\ge A_r(p),
\]

and therefore (8) implies

\[
t(\widehat H,W)
\ge
\frac{A_r(p)^m}
{A_2(p)^{a_2-\ell}
 \displaystyle\prod_{s=3}^{r-1}A_s(p)^{a_s}}
=
p^\ell\Phi_H(p).
\]

Equation (8) is the direct \(K_r\)-analogue of the Grzesik–Lee–Lidický–Volec lemma.

---

## 6. Why the triangle itself has no robustness budget

For \(H=K_3\),

\[
(b_1,b_2,b_3)=(1,1,1),
\]

so

\[
b_3-b_2=0.
\]

There is no edge separator available to compensate for a new maximal \(K_2\).

Attaching twenty leaves at each of the three vertices adds

\[
\ell=60
\]

maximal \(K_2\)'s and gives

\[
(b_1,b_2,b_3)=(1,61,1).
\]

Thus this example lies very far outside the monotone-exponent region. This agrees with the GLLV parameter: for a single triangle,

\[
\kappa(K_3)=0.
\]

In contrast, a book consisting of \(m\) triangles sharing a common edge has \(m-1\) edge separators. It therefore tolerates any pendant forest with at most \(m-1\) total edges. To certify sixty attached edges by this theorem, one may take a triangle edge-tree with at least sixty edge separators—for instance, a book with at least \(61\) triangle pages.

---

## 7. The budget is optimal for the current proof method

This threshold is not only the point at which the monotone exponent condition ceases to hold. It is also the maximal threshold obtainable using only the two abstract pieces of information used in the present proof:

1. the entropy deficits \(\delta_j\) are nondecreasing;
2. their suffix sums satisfy the Moon–Moser bounds.

Indeed, in the strict range define

\[
\lambda_j:=-\log c_j(p),
\]

so that \(\lambda_2<\lambda_3\) for \(p<1\). Consider the abstract deficit sequence

\[
\widetilde\delta_1=0,
\qquad
\widetilde\delta_2=\widetilde\delta_3
=
\frac{\lambda_2+\lambda_3}{2},
\qquad
\widetilde\delta_j=\lambda_j\quad(j\ge4).
\]

It is nondecreasing. It also satisfies every suffix constraint:

- the suffix beginning at \(j=2\) is bounded because
  \((\lambda_2+\lambda_3)/2\le\lambda_3\);
- the suffix beginning at \(j=1\) has equality;
- every later suffix has equality.

Let \(b'_2=b_2+\ell\) and \(b'_j=b_j\) otherwise. Then

\[
\sum_j b'_j\widetilde\delta_j
-
\sum_j b'_j\lambda_j
=
\frac{(b_2+\ell-b_3)(\lambda_3-\lambda_2)}{2}.
\]

This is strictly positive whenever

\[
\ell>b_3-b_2.
\]

Therefore, once the edge budget is exceeded, the desired weighted entropy inequality does not follow from the present monotonicity and suffix estimates alone.

This does **not** prove that the graph inequality must fail immediately beyond the budget. It shows that any extension beyond it requires a genuinely new input—such as an inequality coupling the one- and two-coordinate marginals more strongly, rather than another rearrangement of the existing Moon–Moser bounds.

---

## 8. The same argument gives higher-clique robustness

There is a useful generalisation of the pendant-edge operation.

Suppose a new simplicial vertex is added whose neighbourhood is an existing \(K_{s-1}\). This attaches a new maximal \(K_s\)-bag along a \(K_{s-1}\)-separator. It changes only one exponent:

\[
b_s\longmapsto b_s+1,
\]

and it multiplies the target polynomial by

\[
c_s(p)=1-(s-1)(1-p).
\]

Consequently, for fixed \(2\le s<r\), one may perform up to

\[
b_{s+1}-b_s
\]

such \(K_s\)-leaf attachments while preserving the monotone exponent condition. For \(s=r\), there is no upper-neighbour constraint, so the monotonicity argument places no limit on the number of new \(K_r\)-bags attached along \(K_{r-1}\)'s. The pendant-tree theorem is exactly the case \(s=2\).

The article with this result inserted as Section 6.1 is available here:

[Patched LaTeX source](sandbox:/mnt/data/chordal_entropy_extension_with_robustness.tex)  
[Compiled PDF](sandbox:/mnt/data/chordal_entropy_extension_with_robustness.pdf)  
[Standalone LaTeX insertion](sandbox:/mnt/data/pendant_forest_robustness_insert.tex)

If I'm understanding correctly, you didn't prove tighter result or something similar, but interpreted the existing result in terms of robustness, right? In other words, the graphs that can be proven to satisfy this Goodman style lower bound by entropic theorem is still same. Right?

Yes. Your interpretation is correct, with one important distinction about which theorem we compare against.

Relative to the **monotone-exponent theorem in the current chordal entropy article**, my previous “pendant robustness” result did **not enlarge the class of graphs for which we prove the Goodman-style bound**. It was a structural reinterpretation of the existing condition.

Indeed, the current theorem already says that a chordal graph \(G\) satisfies the desired bound whenever

\[
b_1(G)\le b_2(G)\le\cdots\le b_r(G).
\]

If \(H\) initially satisfies this condition and we add \(\ell\) pendant edges, then

\[
b(\widehat H)
=
\bigl(b_1(H),\,b_2(H)+\ell,\,b_3(H),\ldots,b_r(H)\bigr).
\]

Therefore

\[
\ell\le b_3(H)-b_2(H)
\]

is **exactly** the condition ensuring that \(\widehat H\) still satisfies the original monotonicity hypothesis. The proof I gave literally concludes “thus \(\widehat H\) satisfies the monotone exponent condition, so Theorem 1 applies.” fileciteturn6file0

So there is no new graph here:

\[
\boxed{
\text{pendant robustness corollary}
\subseteq
\text{graphs already covered by the monotone-exponent theorem}.
}
\]

The direct projected-edge entropy calculation I gave later produces a somewhat stronger **intermediate inequality**

\[
t(\widehat H,W)
\ge
\frac{t_r^m}
{t_2^{a_2-\ell}\prod_{s=3}^{r-1}t_s^{a_s}},
\]

but after applying Moon–Moser it gives the same final class \(\ell\le a_2\). It does not permit even one more pendant edge beyond what the \(b\)-monotonicity condition already permits. fileciteturn6file7

### Where GLLV is genuinely different

This also clarifies why the Grzesik–Lee–Lidický–Volec paper initially looked more interesting. Their Theorem 1.1 says every triangle-tree is common, while Theorem 1.2 says that under the quantitative condition

\[
2e(H)-3v(H)+3\ge t,
\]

one may attach **any tree with at most \(t\) edges** and retain commonality. The resulting graph is generally no longer a triangle-tree. Thus, relative to their preceding triangle-tree theorem, Theorem 1.2 really is a robustness enlargement. fileciteturn5file0

But our newer monotone-exponent theorem has already enlarged the chordal class enough that precisely those pendant extensions are automatically included. In the triangle-tree case,

\[
b_3-b_2=\kappa(H)=2e(H)-3v(H)+3,
\]

so the two thresholds coincide. What GLLV presents as a robustness phenomenon has effectively already been absorbed into our structural condition.

### So the interesting question is stronger

What we actually want is something like this:

> Start with a chordal \(H\) satisfying
> \[
> b_1\le\cdots\le b_r,
> \]
> and add \(\ell\) pendant edges with
> \[
> \boxed{\ell>b_3-b_2}.
> \]
> Can the Goodman-style inequality nevertheless remain true for some nonzero range beyond this threshold?

That would be a **genuine robustness theorem** for our result, because the resulting graph would fail the hypothesis of the existing theorem.

For example, if \(H\) is pure and has \(a_2\) edge-separators, our current theorem certifies only

\[
\ell\le a_2.
\]

A genuinely new statement would look like

\[
\ell\le C(H)
\qquad\text{with}\qquad
C(H)>a_2,
\]

or perhaps a multiplicative/asymptotic estimate such as

\[
\ell\le (1+\varepsilon)a_2,
\qquad
\ell\le c\,m,
\]

under additional structural hypotheses.

There is another useful point from the previous analysis: using **only** the entropy-deficit monotonicity and the Moon–Moser suffix bounds in the current proof, one cannot pass the threshold \(b_3-b_2\); the abstract deficit construction shows those inputs cease to imply the desired inequality once \(b_2+\ell>b_3\). fileciteturn6file9 So a genuine robustness result requires a new inequality linking the marginal entropies more tightly—not merely a different rearrangement of the current proof.

I think this is now the right problem to attack: **how far beyond \(b_3-b_2\) can pendant edges be tolerated?** In particular, the first nontrivial laboratory is probably a pure triangle-tree with \(a\) edge-separators and \(a+1\) pendant edges. If we can prove even that one-extra-edge case under some structural assumptions, that would be a genuinely stronger theorem rather than a reformulation.

Consider graphs with at most 6 vertices, no isolated edge or isolated vertex (they wouldn't affect the lower bound stated in the file), that are non-bipartite (which is target of the lower bound stated in the file). 
How many graphs satisfy the condition stated in the file among them?
I’ll inspect the TeX file to extract the exact graph condition, then enumerate unlabeled graphs on up to six vertices and report the count with enough detail to verify the interpretation.

The file’s operative hypothesis is: chordal, clique number at least \(3\), and the clique-factor exponents satisfy \(b_1\le \cdots\le b_r\). I’m checking both the connected reading used explicitly in the paper and the natural componentwise/disconnected extension, since your exclusion of isolated vertices and isolated edges suggests the latter may be intended.

Interpreting “graphs” as **unlabeled simple graphs**, the answer is:

\[
\boxed{30}
\]

I counted graphs \(H\) satisfying:

- \(v(H)\le 6\);
- no isolated vertices;
- no connected component is \(K_2\);
- \(H\) is non-bipartite;
- \(H\) is chordal;
- the exponent sequence from the file satisfies
  \[
  b_1\le b_2\le\cdots\le b_{\omega(H)}.
  \]

The count by number of vertices is:

| \(v(H)\) | Count |
|---:|---:|
| 3 | 1 |
| 4 | 2 |
| 5 | 7 |
| 6 | 20 |
| **Total** | **30** |

The only disconnected graph counted is \(K_3\sqcup K_3\), whose exponent sequence is \((2,2,2)\).

Strictly following the file’s standing assumption that \(H\) is connected gives instead

\[
\boxed{29}.
\]

For connected graphs, the counts are \(1,2,7,19\) for \(3,4,5,6\) vertices, respectively.

prompts.text: **# ChatGPT Pro proof task: three unresolved chordal Atlas graphs** **## Instructions to the proof model** Treat this entire document as a research request and begin the mathematical work immediately. Do not merely summarize the prompt or return a list of possible approaches. Your primary task is to prove or refute at least one of the three Goodman-style graphon inequalities below. Start with the concrete Atlas 181 lemma \\[ t(H\_{181},W)\stackrel{?}{\geq}(2p-1)^2t(K\_4,W), \qquad p=t(K\_2,W)\geq\frac23. \\] If it is true, give a complete proof for arbitrary graphons. If it is false, give an explicit weighted finite-step graphon and verify the violation exactly. If you cannot settle it, do not stop at saying that the problem is difficult: prove the strongest correct intermediate lemma you can, identify the exact remaining implication, and then try Atlas 157 or Atlas 130. **### PDFs supplied with this prompt** Read the attached files before proving anything that depends on them. You may cite a proved result from an attachment as a lemma, but identify its precise statement and verify that all of its hypotheses apply here. 1\. **\*\*Required:\*\*** \chordal\_entropy\_extension.pdf\. This contains    the proved common-\\(K\_r\\)-law entropy theorem, its deficit formulation,    the Moon--Moser suffix inequalities, and the PAVA bound. 2\. **\*\*Recommended for Atlas 157:\*\***    \paw\_triangle\_edge\_cones.pdf\. This is the accepted proof    covering Atlas 49, obtained from Atlas 157 by deleting its leaf. 3\. **\*\*Optional supporting-plane references:\*\***    \atlas160\_k4\_paw\_edge\_supporting\_plane.pdf\ and    \atlas178\_half\_degree\_weighted\_k4.pdf\. These show two    successful weighted-\\(K\_4\\) arguments for nearby classified graphs. The prompt itself contains the graph definitions, targets, and proposed reductions, so no classification spreadsheet or Atlas software is needed. If only one PDF can be attached, attach \chordal\_entropy\_extension.pdf\ and work on Atlas 181. **## Purpose** This note isolates the three chordal graphs still not fully classified for \\[ t(H,W)\geq \Phi\_H(p) :=(1-p)^{v(H)}\chi\_H\\!\left(\frac1{1-p}\right), \qquad p=t(K\_2,W), \\] throughout the required Turán interval \\[ p\geq 1-\frac1{\chi(H)-1}. \\] They are NetworkX Graph Atlas 130, 157, and 181. All statements sought below are for arbitrary graphons and homomorphism densities. A graphon is a symmetric measurable function \\(W:[0,1]^2\to[0,1]\\). For a finite graph \\(F\\), \\[ t(F,W)= \int\_{[0,1]^{V(F)}} \prod\_{uv\in E(F)}W(x\_u,x\_v) \prod\_{u\in V(F)}dx\_u. \\] Thus all densities here are ordinary homomorphism densities, not injective densities. **## Notation and the existing theorem** Put \\[ c\_1=1,\qquad c\_2=p,\qquad c\_3=2p-1=\:r,\qquad c\_4=3p-2=\:s. \\] For a chordal graph, choose a clique tree and define \\[ b\_j= \\#\\{\text{maximal cliques of size at least }j\\} -\\#\\{\text{clique-tree separators of size at least }j\\}. \\] Then \\[ \Phi\_H(p)=\prod\_j c\_j^{b\_j}. \\] The current theorem proves this target whenever \\[ b\_1\leq b\_2\leq\cdots\leq b\_{\omega(H)}. \\] For an arbitrary chordal graph, pool-adjacent-violators replaces \\(b\\) by its nondecreasing pooling \\(\bar b\\) and proves only \\[ t(H,W)\geq \Psi\_H(p):=\prod\_j c\_j^{\bar b\_j} \leq \Phi\_H(p). \\] The loss caused by that pooling is the exact obstruction in all three cases. **## Exact census** \| Atlas | graph6 | Description | \\(\chi\_H(x)\\) | Required target | \|---:|---|---|---|---| \| 130 | \E{CW\ | Two triangles joined by one bridge | \\(x(x-1)^3(x-2)^2\\) | \\(p^3r^2,\ p\geq1/2\\) | \| 157 | \E\~`\_\ | A \\(K\_4\\), a triangle page on one clique edge, and a leaf at a clique vertex outside that edge | \\(x(x-1)^2(x-2)^2(x-3)\\) | \\(p^2r^2s,\ p\geq2/3\\) | \| 181 | \E^mG\ | A \\(K\_4\\) with triangle pages on two opposite clique edges | \\(x(x-1)(x-2)^3(x-3)\\) | \\(pr^3s,\ p\geq2/3\\) | The respective edge counts are 7, 9, and 10. For an explicit six-vertex input, the Atlas labelings have edge sets \\[ \begin{aligned} E(H\_{130})&=\\{01,02,03,12,34,35,45\\},\\\\ E(H\_{157})&=\\{01,02,03,04,12,13,15,23,25\\},\\\\ E(H\_{181})&=\\{02,03,04,05,12,13,23,24,34,45\\}. \end{aligned} \\] **## Where the current entropy proof stops** **### Atlas 130** The maximal clique sizes are \\((3,3,2)\\); the two clique-tree separators have size \\(1\\). Thus \\[ b=(1,3,2). \\] The jump \\(3>2\\) violates monotonicity. Pooling gives \\[ \bar b=(1,5/2,5/2) \quad\Longrightarrow\quad t(H\_{130},W)\geq p^{5/2}r^{5/2}. \\] The target exceeds this bound by \\[ \frac{\Phi\_{130}}{\Psi\_{130}}=\sqrt{\frac p r}. \\] **### Atlas 157** The maximal clique sizes are \\((4,3,2)\\). The \\(K\_3\\) page meets the \\(K\_4\\) in an edge, and the maximal leaf edge meets it in a vertex. Hence \\[ b=(1,2,2,1). \\] Pooling gives \\[ \bar b=(1,5/3,5/3,5/3) \quad\Longrightarrow\quad t(H\_{157},W)\geq (prs)^{5/3}. \\] The missing factor is \\[ \frac{\Phi\_{157}}{\Psi\_{157}} \=\left(\frac{pr}{s^2}\right)^{1/3}. \\] It diverges as \\(p\downarrow2/3\\), so a uniform constant-factor improvement of the pooled theorem cannot settle the threshold region. **### Atlas 181** The maximal clique sizes are \\((4,3,3)\\), and both separators have size \\(2\\). Therefore \\[ b=(1,1,3,1). \\] Pooling gives \\[ \bar b=(1,1,2,2) \quad\Longrightarrow\quad t(H\_{181},W)\geq pr^2s^2. \\] The missing factor is \\[ \frac{\Phi\_{181}}{\Psi\_{181}}=\frac r s, \\] which again diverges as \\(p\downarrow2/3\\). **## Atlas 130: a surplus-controlled complement correlation** Define the rooted triangle density \\[ \tau(x)=\int W(x,a)W(x,b)W(a,b)\\,da\\,db, \qquad T=\int\tau(x)\\,dx=t(K\_3,W). \\] Then \\[ t(H\_{130},W) \=\int\tau(x)W(x,y)\tau(y)\\,dx\\,dy. \\] Goodman's inequality gives \\(T\geq pr\\). With \\(U=1-W\\), set \\[ B:=\int U(x,y)\tau(x)\tau(y)\\,dx\\,dy. \\] We have the exact identity \\[ t(H\_{130},W)=T^2-B. \\] Writing the Goodman surplus as \\[ \delta:=T-pr\geq0, \\] the desired Atlas 130 bound follows from the concrete statement below. \> **\*\*Atlas 130 target lemma.\*\*** For every graphon with \\(p\geq1/2\\), \> \\[ \> B-(1-p)T^2\leq 2p^2r\delta+p\delta^2. \> \\] Indeed, \\[ T^2-B \geq pT^2-2p^2r\delta-p\delta^2 \=p^3r^2. \\] The tempting stronger claim \\(t(H\_{130},W)\geq pT^2\\) should not be assumed: existing finite-step numerical diagnostics found violations. The useful object is the Goodman surplus, not unconditional positive correlation of the rooted triangle weights across an edge. Possible routes: 1\. Express \\(\delta\\) through complement-degree variance and mixed    triangles, then control the excess \\(B-(1-p)T^2\\) by those terms. 2\. Find a supporting plane for the rooted variables \\(d=T\_W1\\),    \\(a=T\_Wd\\), and \\(\tau\\). 3\. Average quantitative certificates associated with the seven positive    edge deletions of Atlas 130. 4\. Search directly for a flag-SOS certificate for the target lemma. **## Atlas 157: retain the surplus from Atlas 49** Label the \\(K\_4\\) vertices \\(a,b,c,d\\). Let the page vertex be adjacent to \\(b,c\\), and attach the leaf at \\(a\\). \tag{7}
\]
\[
d\alpha(x,y)=\frac{W(x,y)C(x,y)}{t_3}\,dx\,dy,
\tag{8}
\]
and
\[
d\beta(x,y)=\frac{W(x,y)Q(x,y)}{t_4}\,dx\,dy.
\tag{9}
\]
Thus \(\lambda\) is the uniform \(W\)-edge law, \(\alpha\) is the distinguished-edge marginal of the uniform triangle law, and \(\beta\) is an edge marginal of the uniform ordered \(K_4\) law.

Put
\[
m=\frac{t_3}{p}.
\tag{10}
\]
Goodman gives \(m\ge r\).

Let \(\mu_4\) be the uniform ordered \(K_4\) law. Then
\[
\frac{h_{181}}{t_4}
=
\mathbb E_{\mu_4}\bigl[C(X_1,X_2)C(X_3,X_4)\bigr].
\tag{11}
\]
By Jensen's inequality and the symmetry of \(\mu_4\),
\[
\frac{h_{181}}{t_4}
\ge
\exp\left(
2\int \log C\,d\beta
\right).
\tag{12}
\]
There is no zero-denominator issue here: \(Q>0\) implies \(C>0\), and \(Q\le C^2\) also gives the required logarithmic integrability.

Define the mismatch deficit
\[
\Delta
=
D(\beta\Vert\alpha)-D(\beta\Vert\lambda).
\tag{13}
\]
Since
\[
\frac{d\alpha}{d\lambda}=\frac{C}{m},
\]
we have the exact identity
\[
D(\beta\Vert\lambda)-D(\beta\Vert\alpha)
=
\int\log\frac{C}{m}\,d\beta.
\tag{14}
\]
Equivalently,
\[
\int\log C\,d\beta=\log m-\Delta.
\tag{15}
\]
Substitution into (12) yields the quantitative bound
\[
\boxed{
h_{181}\ge t_4\,m^2e^{-2\Delta}.
}
\tag{16}
\]

Consequently, the exact additional implication needed by this entropy route is
\[
\boxed{
\Delta\le \log\frac{m}{r}
=
\log\frac{t_3}{pr}.
}
\tag{17}
\]
Indeed, (17) in (16) gives \(h_{181}\ge r^2t_4\).

The stronger opposite-page conjecture would follow from the sharper comparison
\[
D(\beta\Vert\alpha)\le D(\beta\Vert\lambda),
\tag{18}
\]
because (18) is \(\Delta\le0\), and therefore
\[
h_{181}\ge t_4m^2
=
\frac{t_4t_3^2}{p^2}.
\]

Thus the triangle surplus \(m/r=t_3/(pr)\) is exactly the amount by which the \(K_4/K_3\) edge-mismatch divergence is allowed to exceed the \(K_4/K_2\) divergence.

This is the precise remaining implication. The common-\(K_4\)-law suffix inequalities in the supplied entropy theorem do not imply (17): pooling controls only the relevant sum of conditional-entropy increments.

### 2.2 Two unconditional lower bounds

The two KL divergences above separately give useful bounds.

First,
\[
0\le D(\beta\Vert\lambda)
=
\int\log\frac{pQ}{t_4}\,d\beta.
\]
Hence
\[
\int\log Q\,d\beta\ge\log\frac{t_4}{p}.
\]
Using \(Q\le C^2\),
\[
\int\log C\,d\beta
\ge
\frac12\log\frac{t_4}{p}.
\]
Together with (12),
\[
\boxed{
h_{181}\ge\frac{t_4^2}{p}.
}
\tag{19}
\]

Second,
\[
0\le D(\beta\Vert\alpha)
=
\int\log\frac{Q}{C}\,d\beta+\log\frac{t_3}{t_4}.
\]
Since \(Q/C\le C\),
\[
0
\le
D(\beta\Vert\alpha)
\le
\int\log C\,d\beta+\log\frac{t_3}{t_4}.
\]
Therefore
\[
\int\log C\,d\beta\ge\log\frac{t_4}{t_3},
\]
and (12) gives
\[
\boxed{
h_{181}\ge\frac{t_4^3}{t_3^2}.
}
\tag{20}
\]

This proves (1).

In particular, the page lemma is already proved whenever either
\[
t_4\ge pr^2
\tag{21}
\]
or
\[
t_4\ge r\,t_3.
\tag{22}
\]
Any counterexample to the page lemma must therefore satisfy simultaneously
\[
t_4<pr^2,\qquad t_4<rt_3,
\tag{23}
\]
as well as the strict entropy-mismatch inequality
\[
\Delta>\log\frac{t_3}{pr}.
\tag{24}
\]

For the original Atlas 181 target, (19) proves
\[
h_{181}\ge pr^3s
\]
whenever
\[
t_4\ge p\,r^{3/2}s^{1/2}.
\tag{25}
\]

At the minimum \(t_4=prs\), (19) gives
\[
h_{181}\ge pr^2s^2,
\]
which is exactly the pooled PAVA bound.

### 2.3 Exact rational test: opposite-page covariance can be negative

Consider the two-step graphon with block masses \(1/2,1/2\) and matrix
\[
W=
\begin{pmatrix}
1&1\\
1&0
\end{pmatrix}.
\tag{26}
\]
Write the blocks as \(A,B\). Then
\[
p=\frac34,\qquad r=\frac12.
\]

The only \(K_4\) types are \(AAAA\) and those with exactly one \(B\), so
\[
t_4=\frac1{16}+\frac4{16}=\frac5{16}.
\tag{27}
\]
The relevant codegrees are
\[
C_{AA}=1,\qquad C_{AB}=\frac12.
\tag{28}
\]

For the one-page density
\[
J=\int K_4(a,b,c,d)C(a,b),
\]
the all-\(A\) contribution is \(1/16\). For a \(K_4\) with one \(B\), the distinguished edge is \(AA\) in two of the four label positions and \(AB\) in the other two. Hence
\[
J
=
\frac1{16}
+
\frac2{16}\cdot1
+
\frac2{16}\cdot\frac12
=
\frac14.
\tag{29}
\]

For two opposite pages, a one-\(B\) \(K_4\) always has one opposite \(AA\) edge and one opposite \(AB\) edge. Therefore
\[
h_{181}
=
\frac1{16}
+
\frac4{16}\cdot\frac12
=
\frac3{16}.
\tag{30}
\]
Consequently,
\[
h_{181}t_4=\frac{15}{256}
<
\frac{16}{256}=J^2.
\tag{31}
\]
Thus the tempting clique-weighted positive-correlation assertion
\[
h_{181}t_4\ge J^2
\]
is false, even for a rational \(0\)-\(1\) two-step graphon.

The desired inequalities nevertheless hold:
\[
h_{181}=\frac3{16}
>
\frac14\cdot\frac5{16}
=
r^2t_4.
\tag{32}
\]
Also \(t_3=1/2\), and
\[
p^2h_{181}=\frac{27}{256}
>
\frac{20}{256}
=
t_4t_3^2.
\tag{33}
\]

This calculation rules out the direct covariance route but does not refute either page statement.

### 2.4 The page lemma for regular graphons

Suppose
\[
d(x)=\int W(x,y)\,dy=p
\quad\text{for a.e. }x.
\tag{34}
\]
Set \(U=1-W\) and \(q=1-p\). The \(U\)-degree is then \(q\) almost everywhere.

Define
\[
D_U(x,y)=\int U(x,z)U(y,z)\,dz.
\]
Expanding \(C\) in the complement gives
\[
C(x,y)
=
1-q-q+D_U(x,y)
=
r+D_U(x,y).
\tag{35}
\]
Therefore
\[
C(x,y)\ge r
\quad\text{for all relevant }(x,y).
\tag{36}
\]
It follows pointwise that
\[
C(a,b)C(c,d)\ge r^2.
\]
Multiplying by the \(K_4\) kernel and integrating yields
\[
\boxed{
h_{181}\ge r^2t_4
}
\tag{37}
\]
for every regular graphon.

No correlation assertion is involved.

If \(t_4>0\) and equality holds in (37), then
\[
D_U(a,b)=D_U(c,d)=0
\]
for \(\mu_4\)-almost every ordered \(K_4\); by symmetry this holds for every edge position of the \(K_4\).

### 2.5 The page lemma for every complete multipartite graphon

Let \(W\) be a complete multipartite graphon with part masses
\[
a_1,a_2,\ldots,\qquad \sum_i a_i=1.
\]
First assume finitely many positive parts. Let \(e_j\) denote the \(j\)-th elementary symmetric polynomial in the \(a_i\). Then
\[
p=2e_2,\qquad t(K_j,W)=j!e_j.
\tag{38}
\]

A \(K_4\) uses four distinct parts \(i,j,k,\ell\). For an edge joining parts \(i,j\),
\[
C_{ij}=1-a_i-a_j.
\]
Hence
\[
h_{181}
=
\sum_{\substack{i,j,k,\ell\\\text{distinct}}}
a_i a_j a_k a_\ell
(1-a_i-a_j)(1-a_k-a_\ell).
\tag{39}
\]

For a four-element set \(S\), write \(a_S=\prod_{i\in S}a_i\). Expanding (39), and using
\[
\sum_{|S|=4}a_S\sum_{i\in S}a_i=e_4-5e_5,
\tag{40}
\]
and
\[
\sum_{|S|=4}a_S\sum_{\{i,j\}\subseteq S}a_i a_j
=
e_2e_4-4e_5+9e_6,
\tag{41}
\]
gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
h_{181}
&=
24e_4-24(e_4-5e_5)
  +16(e_2e_4-4e_5+9e_6)\\
&=
16e_2e_4+56e_5+144e_6.
\end{aligned}
\]
Equivalently,
\[
\boxed{
h_{181}
=
\frac p3\,t_4
+\frac7{15}\,t(K_5,W)
+\frac15\,t(K_6,W).
}
\tag{42}
\]

For completeness, the required clique recurrences can be proved directly in this multipartite setting. Put \(Q=\sum_i a_i^2=1-p\), and write
\[
e_{j-1}^{(i)}
=
e_{j-1}(a_1,\ldots,\widehat{a_i},\ldots).
\]
The identities
\[
e_j
=
(j+1)e_{j+1}
+
\sum_i a_i^2e_{j-1}^{(i)}
\tag{43}
\]
and
\[
\sum_i a_i e_{j-1}^{(i)}=j e_j
\tag{44}
\]
hold.

Moreover,
\[
e_{j-1}^{(i)}-e_{j-1}^{(k)}
=
(a_k-a_i)e_{j-2}^{(i,k)}.
\]
Thus the sequences \(a_i\) and \(e_{j-1}^{(i)}\) are oppositely ordered, and their weighted covariance, with weights \(a_i\), is nonpositive:
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\sum_i a_i^2e_{j-1}^{(i)}
-
\left(\sum_i a_i^2\right)
\left(\sum_i a_i e_{j-1}^{(i)}\right)\\
&\qquad=
\frac12
\sum_{i,k}a_i a_k
(a_i-a_k)
\bigl(e_{j-1}^{(i)}-e_{j-1}^{(k)}\bigr)
\le0.
\end{aligned}
\tag{45}
\]
Therefore
\[
\sum_i a_i^2e_{j-1}^{(i)}
\le
jQe_j.
\]
Using (43),
\[
\frac{(j+1)e_{j+1}}{e_j}
\ge
1-jQ
=
jp-(j-1).
\tag{46}
\]
Thus
\[
t(K_{j+1},W)
\ge
\bigl(jp-(j-1)\bigr)t(K_j,W).
\tag{47}
\]

We now apply (42).

#### \(2/3\le p\le3/4\)

All terms in (42) are nonnegative, so
\[
\frac{h_{181}}{t_4}\ge\frac p3.
\]
But
\[
\frac p3-r^2
=
4\left(p-\frac13\right)\left(\frac34-p\right)
\ge0.
\tag{48}
\]

#### \(3/4\le p\le4/5\)

From (47) with \(j=4\),
\[
t(K_5,W)\ge(4p-3)t_4.
\]
Hence
\[
\frac{h_{181}}{t_4}
\ge
\frac p3+\frac7{15}(4p-3)
=
\frac{11p-7}{5}.
\]
Furthermore,
\[
\frac{11p-7}{5}-r^2
=
4\left(p-\frac34\right)\left(\frac45-p\right)
\ge0.
\tag{49}
\]

#### \(p\ge4/5\)

Now
\[
t(K_5,W)\ge(4p-3)t_4
\]
and
\[
t(K_6,W)\ge(5p-4)t(K_5,W)
\ge(5p-4)(4p-3)t_4.
\]
Therefore
\[
\begin{aligned}
\frac{h_{181}}{t_4}
&\ge
\frac p3
+\frac7{15}(4p-3)
+\frac15(4p-3)(5p-4)\\
&=
4p^2-4p+1\\
&=r^2.
\end{aligned}
\tag{50}
\]

This proves
\[
\boxed{
h_{181}\ge r^2t_4
}
\tag{51}
\]
for every complete multipartite graphon.

Complete multipartite graphons with a diffuse family of null classes follow by replacing the diffuse part by \(N\) equal parts, applying the finite-part result, and passing to the limit. The approximating graphons converge in \(L^1\), and every fixed homomorphism density converges by the usual telescoping estimate.

## 3. Deduction of the original Atlas 181 target

Assume the minimal page lemma
\[
h_{181}\ge r^2t_4.
\]
The supplied Moon–Moser inequalities give
\[
t_3\ge rp
\]
and
\[
t_4\ge s\,t_3.
\]
Consequently
\[
t_4\ge prs.
\]
Therefore
\[
\boxed{
h_{181}
\ge r^2t_4
\ge r^2(prs)
=
pr^3s.
}
\tag{52}
\]

Thus the original Atlas 181 inequality is proved for every regular graphon and every complete multipartite graphon. For arbitrary graphons it remains conditional on (181-page), or on the sufficient entropy-mismatch estimate (17).

## 4. Audit

### \(p=2/3\)

Here
\[
r=\frac13,\qquad s=0.
\]
The original Atlas 181 target is
\[
pr^3s=0,
\]
so it holds trivially for every graphon.

The page lemma is still nontrivial:
\[
h_{181}\ge\frac19t_4.
\]
It is proved above for regular and complete multipartite graphons. If \(t_4=0\), then \(h_{181}=0\) because \(0\le C\le1\) implies \(h_{181}\le t_4\).

No division by \(s\) was made.

### \(p=1\)

Since \(0\le W\le1\) and \(\int W=1\), one has \(W=1\) almost everywhere. Thus
\[
C=1,\qquad t_3=t_4=h_{181}=1,
\]
and both the page lemma and the original target hold with equality.

### Zero \(K_4\)-density

If \(t_4=0\), then \(h_{181}=0\). The probability law \(\beta\) is not introduced in that case.

For \(p>2/3\), (3) gives \(t_4\ge prs>0\), so the zero-\(K_4\) case can occur only at the threshold \(p=2/3\).

### Divisions by \(p,r,t_3,t_4\)

Throughout the Atlas 181 range,
\[
p\ge\frac23,\qquad r\ge\frac13.
\]
Goodman gives
\[
t_3\ge pr>0.
\]
Division by \(t_4\) is made only after treating \(t_4=0\) separately. No division by \(s\) is used.

### Equality cases established

The proofs establish equality in the page lemma and the original target for every balanced complete \(k\)-partite graphon:
\[
p=\frac{k-1}{k},\qquad
r=\frac{k-2}{k},\qquad
s=\frac{k-3}{k}.
\]
Every edge then has codegree \(r\), and
\[
t_4=prs,\qquad
h_{181}=r^2t_4=pr^3s.
\]
This includes \(k=3\), where \(t_4=h_{181}=0\), and the limiting case \(W=1\).

For a regular graphon with \(t_4>0\), equality in the page lemma requires
\[
D_U(x,y)=0
\]
on every \(K_4\)-edge position almost surely under the \(K_4\) law.

For the constant graphon \(W\equiv p\),
\[
C=p^2,\qquad
t_4=p^6,\qquad
h_{181}=p^{10}.
\]
Thus
\[
\frac{h_{181}}{t_4}=p^4\ge r^2,
\]
because
\[
p^2-r=(1-p)^2.
\]
The page inequality is strict unless \(p=1\). The stronger normalized inequality is an equality:
\[
p^2h_{181}=p^{12}=t_4t_3^2.
\]

### 5.1 A unified result for all regular graphons

The regularity identity (35),
\[
C(x,y)=r+D_U(x,y)\ge r,
\]
settles all three targets in the regular setting.

#### Atlas 157

If \(d(a)=p\) almost everywhere, then the covariance term in the prompt vanishes identically:
\[
t(H_{157},W)=pJ.
\]
The precise Atlas 49 result proved in `paw_triangle_edge_cones.pdf` is
\[
J\ge pr^2s,\qquad p\ge\frac23.
\]
Therefore
\[
\boxed{
t(H_{157},W)\ge p^2r^2s
}
\tag{53}
\]
for every regular graphon.

Equivalently, one can avoid the Atlas 49 result here: since \(C(b,c)\ge r\),
\[
t(H_{157},W)
\ge pr\,t_4
\ge p^2r^2s.
\]

For a nonregular graphon, putting \(x=d-p\) and
\[
V=\int x^2,
\]
the exact decomposition is
\[
t(H_{157},W)=pJ+\mathcal E_{157},
\]
where
\[
\mathcal E_{157}
=
\int K_4(a,b,c,d)C(b,c)x(a).
\]
Since the rooted factor multiplying \(x(a)\) lies in \([0,1]\),
\[
\mathcal E_{157}
\ge-\int x_-
\ge-\frac12\sqrt V.
\tag{54}
\]
Hence the rigorous near-regular estimate
\[
\boxed{
t(H_{157},W)
\ge
p^2r^2s-\frac12\sqrt{\operatorname{Var}(d)}.
}
\tag{55}

To obtain the full result from this route, the Atlas 49 surplus would need to control the negative part of \(\mathcal E_{157}\). The regular proof shows that this is purely a degree-irregularity obstruction.

### 5.2 Atlas 130 is proved for every regular graphon, with surplus

Assume now \(p\ge1/2\) and \(d(x)=p\) almost everywhere. Put
\[
q=1-p,\qquad
A=pr.
\]
As above,
\[
C(x,y)=r+D_U(x,y).
\]

The rooted triangle density satisfies
\[
\begin{aligned}
\tau(x)
&=\int W(x,y)C(x,y)\,dy\\
&=pr+g(x),
\end{aligned}
\tag{56}
\]
where
\[
g(x)=\int W(x,y)D_U(x,y)\,dy\ge0.
\tag{57}
\]
Since \(T=\int\tau\),
\[
\delta=T-pr=\int g.
\tag{58}
\]

Recall
\[
B=\int U(x,y)\tau(x)\tau(y)\,dx\,dy.
\]
Because the \(U\)-degree is the constant \(q\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
B
&=
qA^2
+2A\int U(x,y)g(x)\,dx\,dy
+\int U(x,y)g(x)g(y)\,dx\,dy\\
&=
qA^2+2qA\delta
+\int U(x,y)g(x)g(y)\,dx\,dy.
\end{aligned}
\tag{59}
\]
Using \(0\le U\le1\) and \(g\ge0\),
\[
\int U(x,y)g(x)g(y)\,dx\,dy
\le
\left(\int g\right)^2
=
\delta^2.
\tag{60}
\]
Therefore
\[
B\le qA^2+2qA\delta+\delta^2.
\tag{61}
\]
Equivalently,
\[
B-qT^2\le p\delta^2.
\tag{62}
\]
This is stronger than the Atlas 130 target lemma
\[
B-qT^2\le2p^2r\delta+p\delta^2.
\]

Finally,
\[
\begin{aligned}
t(H_{130},W)
&=T^2-B\\
&\ge
(A+\delta)^2-
\bigl(qA^2+2qA\delta+\delta^2\bigr)\\
&=
pA^2+2pA\delta\\
&=
\boxed{
p^3r^2+2p^2r\delta
}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{63}
\]
In particular,
\[
\boxed{
t(H_{130},W)\ge p^3r^2
}
\tag{64}
\]
for every regular graphon.

This argument also handles \(p=1/2\): then \(r=A=0\), and it gives \(t(H_{130},W)\ge0\).

For an arbitrary graphon, let
\[
x=d-p,\qquad V=\int x^2,
\]
and retain
\[
g(z)=\int W(z,y)D_U(z,y)\,dy\ge0.
\]
A direct expansion gives
\[
\boxed{
\tau(z)
=
pr
+(3p-1)x(z)
+x(z)^2
+(T_Wx)(z)
+g(z).
}
\tag{65}
\]
Furthermore,
\[
\delta
=
2V+\int g.
\tag{66}
\]
Thus the regular proof removes exactly the signed term
\[
(3p-1)x+x^2+T_Wx.
\]
Controlling its \(U\)-quadratic correlation with the nonnegative remainder \(g\) is the remaining Atlas 130 implication. Merely bounding the variance of \(x\) loses a square root and does not recover the required linear dependence on \(\delta\).

### 5.3 A quantitative arbitrary-graphon degree reduction for Atlas 181

For arbitrary \(W\), write
\[
x(z)=d(z)-p,\qquad e(z)=x(z)_-=(p-d(z))_+.
\]
From
\[
C(x,y)=r+x(x)+x(y)+D_U(x,y)
\]
we have
\[
C(x,y)\ge \bigl(r-e(x)-e(y)\bigr)_+.
\]
For \(A,B\ge0\),
\[
(r-A)_+(r-B)_+
\ge
r^2-r(A+B).
\]
Therefore
\[
C(a,b)C(c,d)
\ge
r^2-r\sum_{z\in\{a,b,c,d\}}e(z).
\]
After multiplying by the \(K_4\) kernel and integrating,
\[
h_{181}
\ge
r^2t_4-4r\int e.
\]
Since \(\int x=0\),
\[
\int e=\frac12\int|x|
\le\frac12\sqrt{\int x^2}.
\]
Thus
\[
\boxed{
h_{181}
\ge
r^2t_4-2r\sqrt{\operatorname{Var}(d)}.
}
\tag{67}
\]

Combining this with \(t_4\ge prs\) proves the original Atlas 181 target whenever
\[
\sqrt{\operatorname{Var}(d)}
\le
\frac r2\bigl(t_4-prs\bigr).
\tag{68}
\]

The bound is not sufficient in the near-equality regime because it is of order \(\sqrt{\operatorname{Var}(d)}\). The exact regular proof and the complete-multipartite proof show that the true correction should exploit the complement-codegree term \(D_U\), rather than discard it as in (67).
